Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	Mr. Speaker, when I had the honour of addressing the House yesterday afternoon I noticed that several members of the Progressive party were absent. I am glad to see them in their seats again because I purpose to address my remarks more particularly to them. They have not failed to comprehend the exceptional position in which they are now placed; for by reason of the results of the late general election the fate of this parliament, of the government, and of every hon. member in this House, is in the hands of less than thirty members of the Progressive party. Therefore these hon. gentlemen are now placed in a position of grave responsibility. May I add that I am not at all afraid that they will not rightfully discharge that responsibility?
In what I said last night, Mr. Speaker, and in what I may say this afternoon, I wish to emphasize that I am speaking for myself alone. I hold no brief for the government.
I am prone at times to be outspoken, that is one of my numerous defects, and if I should go too far in what I am about to say I wish it to be clearly understood that I am personally responsible and am not voicing the views of the government.
It seems to me that the situation that has been disclosed by hon. members, particularly by those of the Progressive party, if I am to take into consideration the declarations made by some of them, has been based on error and misunderstanding from the very beginning. I have heard hon. members say that if they vote against this amendment, necessarily they vote confidence in the government. On my own responsibility I say that, in so far as I understand the situation, hon. members do not vote confidence in the government should they vote against this amendment.

What is the proposition before the House? Let us be practical; let us be logical. The proposition before the House is presented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), as representing the government, who says in plain language: I move that the Speech from the Throne be considered by this House. What does that mean? It means that hon. gentlemen are asked purely and simply to pass judgment on the Speech from the Throne, and nothing else. The motion does not ask hon. members to vote for the Speech from the Throne. It asks the 245 members of this House simply to discuss and pass judgment upon the Speech from the Throne. It simply asks that the Speech from the Throne come before this House for discussion, and when it does come up for discussion, then any hon. member may vote for or against it just as he pleases. That is the meaning of the proposition, that and nothing else.
What is the meaning of the proposition of the leader of the opposition? What is its purport? I do not intend to analyse his amendment now, because that has been done several times already, but what is its object? Its object is to stop the government right here and now, to say to the government: You shall not go any further; the Speech from the Throne shall not be discussed in this House, and shall not be submitted to a vote of this House. That is the purport and the effect of his amendment, and if his amendment carries the Speech from the Throne will never be submitted to this House. Some Speech from the Throne will no doubt be submitted, but the Speech from the Throne that was read at the beginning of this session will never be submitted to this House. Therefore, I say that if the amendment is rejected, that will not mean that parliament has voted non-confidence in the government because hon. member's, may, if they choose, vote against the amendment, thereby ensuring that the Speech from the Throne will be submitted to a vote of this House, and then, when it is so submitted, hon. members who have voted against the amendment may turn and vote against the Speech from the Throne if it does not suit them, and there will be no contradiction in that at all. That is the reason why I say that the amendment of the leader of the opposition at this juncture is premature. It is premature in so far as it seems inequitable that the Speech from the Throne should not be submitted to this House, and more particularly does it seem inequitable to the Progressive party, because if the .amendment carried it would prevent the Speech from being even discussed by the House. The amendment is not premature so far as the

Conservative party is concerned, because it is their avowed purpose to defeat the government on the first opportunity. Irrespective of their programme, irrespective of the Speech from the Throne, irrespective of any other consideration, they are here to defeat the government. I do not blame them for trying to do so, but so far as the Progressive party is concerned, a party which is supposed to occupy an independent position between the two great parties, and which I am sure is independent, and which is not committed to the defeat of the government but is committed to the interests of the country at large, and the interests of their own constituencies in particular, I say that for that party the amendment is premature, because, if carried, it precludes consideration of the Speech from the Throne, which is a very worthy document from the Progressive point of view.

I do not apply this quotation to hon. gentlemen opposite who have indulged in applause. It is for the benefit of the members of the Progressive party. I spoke for the benefit of the members of the Progressive party. In the face of this situation, if they prevent this House from considering the Speech from the Throne, they will not be doing justice either to their constituents or themselves, because the Speech from the Throne embodies their desires. I have not heard a single member of the Progressive parly so far state that he was displeased with the Speech from the Throne. Perhaps my hon. friends to my left do not like this remark, but if members of the Progressive party are satisfied, as I think they are, with the Speech from the Throne, they should not prevent its consideration if they do not want to place themselves in direct contradiction to their principles and their polities. A different proposition will be submitted when the time comes to vote on the Speech from the Throne; but at the present time the Speech is deserving of the attention of this House, and of the attention of the Progressive party, irrespective of the conduct, good or bad, of the Liberal party for the past four years, and irrespective of the confidence or the non-confidence of hon. members in that group in the ability of. the government to conduct the affaire of the government for the future. The Speech is a working document and should be submitted to the House. That is my proposition and hon. members will be doing a greater injury to themselves than to anyone else in the House if they object to the consideration of the Speech from the Throne, and will be accountable to their constituents. It has been said by the highest authority that those whom the gods wish to ruin they first deprive of their senses.
The hon. member for Kindersley has advanced arguments which to my mind seem to be lacking in logic and in justice, and I think that they show inability to grasp the situation. Whether these gentlemen are satisfied or not with what they have received

Government's Right to Office
in the past is not the question. If they are not satisfied, is that a reason why they should now prevent the government from putting into effect the provisions contained in the Speech from the Throne, if those provisions are agreeable to them? I should prefer to have them say "We are not pleased with the Speech from the Throne" than to take the ground that some of them have taken. If they are not satisfied with the Speech, they might as well kill it on a vote of want of confidence as to let the House discuss it for three weeks and kill it afterwards. But if they are satisfied with the Speech from the Throne, party considerations should not prevent them from considering it and voting on it. The hon. member for Kindersley said in effect "Let us judge their future from their past. 'In the past they did not implement their promises; therefore they will not implement them in the future". The answer to that is that the government is only one party in the House and1 cannot carry on the business of the country without the help of some other party, and the Progressive party can, at any time in the future, defeat a government that does not implement its promises as contained in the Speech from the Throne. Why should they prejudice the situation and say that they will not do this, or they will not do that, when the Speech from the Throne has not even been discussed? Let us discuss it and consider it if we can; then it will be the duty of the government to implement the Speech from the Throne, and if they do not carry out its provisions the Progressive party may logically say, "We have given you full opportunity to implement your promises and you have not done so. We have no more confidence in you, and therefore we will withdraw our support". That would be logical and would be worthy of any party and1 I for one would not rise from my seat in the House to criticize such a proposition.
I have endeavoured to point out the illogical situation which would be created if this amendment were adopted. If the amendment carries the government cannot remain longer in office; if the government with their Speech from the Throne are thrown out of power and the Conservative party come into power, then the Progressives will have to accept what they will receive from the Conservative party, whether they like it or not, or else go to the polls and have another general election. Is it expedient that we should have another general election? I do not think it is. I do not think the people want it. If the people want the business of the country carried on they do not want another general election.
To use a famous word, the people of this country want tranquillity. Now that the business of the country is increasing rapidly andi confidence is being restored, all classes want tranquility.

I will say both.
I am speaking of tranquillity now-tranquillity first and stability afterwards, or both together if you want it. Tranquillity was a famous word in England when Bonar Law a few years ago ran an election and defeated Lloyd George and Asquith with that slogan "tranquillity." The English people wanted peace. They wanted progress and tranquillity. They thought they would get it under Bonar Law and voted for him. We want tranquillity, and therefore we do not want any general election, but not on account of such petty considerations as that some members of parliament might not be returned or might lose their indemnity. Members of parliament are much too high and lofty to have such ideas, and I deprecate any such consideration. We do not want any general election because the people do not want it. That is the chief reason, and besides it would be contrary to the interests of the country. Should the government be thrown out of power the only alternatives are to support the Conservative government, good or bad, or to have a general election.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) the other day said-not in so many words, but I take it this was his meaning:
' Well! let us turn out this government."

My hon. friends
on your left, Sir, may take this as they like. It is not, perhaps, so much against them as they may think. We want tranquillity and not a general election. Ontario wants tran-

Government's Right to Office
quillity; Quebec wants tranquillity, and Quebec and Ontario combined represent 147 members. The other members of this House also want tranquillity. Even were I not a supporter of the Liberal party, just because of this desire for tranquillity I would express this opinion: that the Liberal party should be left in power until such time as, by reason of their specific actions, the parliament of Canada lose confidence in them. The fact that they have returned here with only 101 members is no reason for an election. A party numbering 101 members is no better and no worse than a party numbering 116, because neither of the two parties can govern with the support only of their own followers. The Liberal party can command the support of only 101 members and the Conservative party can command the support of but 116 members. They have to make-call it what you like-alliances, adhesions, but they must get support from somebody else. That is the reason why I say we want tranquillity, not because I am a partisan, but using my judgment to the best of my ability. I have always thought and I still believe the Progressive party will give their support to the Liberal party, because the Liberal party is nearer to the Progressives than the Conservatives are. Perhaps I shall be accused of speaking as a partisan, but I am not; any man who knows political policies in this country must admit that the Progressives are nearer to the Liberals than the Conservatives are. Shall I give an illustration? I should not like to be discourteous to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), but we all know what he said one day in this House, and I am quoting this only to establish my position. At the time to which I refer, my hon. friends were called the Farmers' party, and the right hon. gentleman said that the Farmers' party w'as only a dilapidated annex of the Liberal party.
I am not saying this with any view of inflicting undue criticism. I bring it forth as a declaration from the leader of the opposition himself that he recognized that the Liberal party and the Progressive party were very much nearer to each other than the Progressive party and the Tory party. This everybody knows, and that is why I say I have always thought and still believe, not because I am a supporter of the Liberal party but basing my conclusion on logic and nothing else, that the Progressive party will give their support to the Liberal party. They have done that more or less for the last four years.

When I say at once that the general tone of this debate has been of a very high order I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that I shall carry with me not only your judgment but, as well, the judgment of hon. members in all parts of the House. We have discussed this question from a highly technical, legal and constitutional point of view; it has been discussed most ably and, indeed, brilliantly by some of the leading lawyers in this House, gentlemen who have attained a very high place in legal circles not only in this country but, I may add, in other parts of the empire as well. Commencing with my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen), who opened the debate, followed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), the debate has resulted in perhaps as fine an exposition of the technical and constitutional aspects of the question under consideration as one could very well wish to hear. We have had as well some very clear cut views from what I might term the layman's standpoint. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) led off this phase of the debate with an address which I am sure from the point of view of the sincerity of the hon. gentleman's opinions must have impressed every member of the House, while his capacity as a layman to weigh the problem and place it fairly before the House was undoubtedly marked. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) made also a notable contribution to the debate, as did the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), from the layman's point of view. We were all delighted with the magnificent oration delivered by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who, returning after so many years' absence, must have cheered your heart, Mr. Speaker. I have no doubt that the older members of the House without exception, who remember the hon. gentleman's style of years
ago, were pleased to listen again to such a brilliant speech as he gave us the other day.
Let me pay my respects to the hon. member
who has just preceded me (Mr. Denis, Joli-ette). Whenever the hon. member rises to address this House-and I say this with the utmost sincerity-he always impresses us, at least those of us who have known him for so many years, with the candor of his views, a quality to which emphasis was given in the closing remarks of his speech. I will not attempt to compete with the hon. member in holding out attractive offers. He suggested that our friends to my left should hasten to grasp the offer he made them, and when he made that suggestion it occurred to me that there is a certain weed which, if you grasp it firmly, will not poison you, but which, if you touch it gently or caressingly is capable of inflicting a sharp pain. Let me tell my hon. friends that even if they grasp quickly and firmly this weed which the hon. member for Joliette is holding out to them, it is still a weed and still carries poison with it.
My hon. friend toward the close of his remarks said that we ought to discuss the Speech from the Throne. Well, I would remind him that his temporary leader in this House who is assuming to represent the government (Mr. Lapointe) has already expressed the opinion that wTe should not discuss the Speech from the Throne until he and his colleagues
4 p.m. and an absentee prime minister have received a vote of confidence.
I shall deal with that suggestion at the proper time. The hon. member for Joliette took very good care to say to-day that he spoke for himself and himself alone. I rather imagine, however-and I think you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, knowing as you do something of the intricacies of party control-that since six o'clock yesterday evening, when my hon. friend made certain statements without that qualification, he must have had several interviews with some of his leaders and been cautioned not to commit the party to anything. They must have said to him. "If you make these suggestions again to-morrow be careful that you indicate that you are speaking for yourself alone." But I wTould ask the hon. member, for whom I have the greatest respect, what is there behind the offer of a policy when it comes from an individual member speaking in his private capacity? I would follow the hon. gentleman a step further in his somewhat extraordinary views and his strained logic.

If my hon. friend will pardon the interruption, I am glad to be able to assure him unhesitatingly that I have not spoken

to any of my party leaders since last night. I had in my notes while I was speaking on that occasion a similar statement to that which I made this afternoon, but, as it happened, I overlooked it at the time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to
accept unreservedly my hon. friend's word in this regard, but we still have his assurance that he has been speaking for himself. And that is the point I am making; he confirms my own judgment upon it. The hon. member declared not only last night but to-day as well that the amendment of my right hon. leader- which I shall not refer to in any detail, seeing that we all have a fairly accurate idea of it- is a motion of want of confidence in the government. We agree; the whole House, I think, is agreed on that point: it is a motion of want of confidence in the government. But the hon. member goes on to say that if we vote against that motion, the vote thus registered will not constitute an expression of confidence in the government. For the life of me I am unable-it may be because I have merely a layman's mind, although I have had an experience in parliament of over fifteen years-to follow the hon. gentleman in this. With all the study I have been able to give to the subject as a layman I cannot understand how it is possible to vote upon a motion one way and imiply a certain conviction and to vote upon it the contrary way and not imply the opposite. The hon. member says that if you vote upon it one way it means one thing, but if you vote upon it the opposite way it is utterly meaningless. I call to my assistance the judgment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), whose eloquence cannot be denied and who generally speaking is logical, although personally 1 seldom agree with the subject matter of his speeches. That hon. member, speaking in this House a year ago, declared that there were only two ways of voting on a given question-yes or no. 1 submit that one of the fundamental principles of parliamentary procedure is this inevitable obligation on the part of members to vote yes or no. It is impossible for one to vote partly yes and partly no; one cannot shade one's opinion in a vote. We must all have the courage to Stand in our places and declare ourselves upon the measure before us.
Mr. Speaker, as I proceed with my observations this afternoon I address myself to every member of this House. I address myself to hon. gentlemen to your right, to hon. gentlemen immediately to your left, and to others who claim the position of being independent of these two parties. I address my-

self to members of this House generally, and I want that fact clearly understood throughout the course of my remarks. I would that I could persuade the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) for instance, or the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) and others to accept the views I shall put forward. I have not much hope of doing so, but I think I shall carry their judgment if I do not carry their vote in the matter.
Let us examine briefly the amendment containing as it does the subject matter of this discussion. It embraces five divisions, and on the first four I think the House is agreed. I will just run over them hastily without quoting them at length: that government candidates were defeated in large numbers; that nine ministers, including the Prime Minister, were defeated; that the Conservatives have the largest representation in the House and received the largest number of popular votes of any party. In these things we all agree, so we may eliminate them from discussion as far as this motion is concerned. The disputed point is this: whether or not those who now assume to advise His Excellency, are competent to do so under the constitution. It is of supreme importance-and I shall deal with that more fully in a moment-whether or not they are competent to act as a committee of parliament. That is the particular point I want to bring to the attention of the House- whether or not a group of gentlemen, three of whose principals are not in this House at all-and I wall name them, Mr. Mackenzie King, Mr. Marler and Mr. Massey-

speechtext: And Mr. Graham.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Graham may be among them, but I understand he has declared his intention of resigning. May I interpolate here that we are all exceedingly sorry to learn of this, because he was a very popular and gracious figure in this House. But those three men who were the directing and most influential spirits in the Liberal party are not in the House. Not only are they not in the House, but they have been rejected at the polls. The people said: We do not want you as the king's advisers. The resolution asks us to declare that this group of individuals, including the three gentlemen to whom I have referred, are not competent to act as a committee of this House commonly known as a government. I do not see, Mr. Speaker, how any hon. member can vote against that declaration. It is simple and clear. We hold that under the constitution they cannot do so. Then we follow with the further declaration that the attempt of this group of individuals to assume the role of advisers of the crown

Government's Right to Office
'is a violation of constitutional practice. That is the gist of the amendment and what it is intended to decide; that and nothing else is what we are considering and what we are voting on. It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that the efforts to resist this amendment, the pleas made against it upon one ground or another, exhibit but the dying gasp of a moribund government. It appears to me that if we face this question frankly there can be but one decision.
'Now I want to bring before the House the utterances of ministers of the crown in order to demonstrate that the position I am taking is the correct one. I have here the, Hansard incorporating the observations of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who assumes to be the leader of the government. I shall quote briefly, but I think the quotations are of importance in view of the change, the somewhat subtle change, which has occurred in the interpretation of the position of hon. gentlemen opposite within the last twenty-four hours. The Minister of Justice, when this amendment was first moved-but let me go further back. When the Minister of Justice made his own motion of confidence, this is what he said:
I should not like anybody to be taken by surprise, and if it is the wish of the House that the consideration of this motion should be postponed till Monday I am quite content to agree, provided the motion is disposed of before we take up any other business.
That was the proviso, that the motion of confidence be disposed of before taking up any other business. That is the first official declaration of him who assumes to lead the government in this House-not on our amendment, but on his own motion. It may be argued, Mr. Speaker, that I am speaking beside the point because that motion is not before us. That may be true. Then let us see what he says in regard to this amendment. On page 25 of Hansard I find these words:
I say that this government does not want to remain in office one day or one hour, unless the parliament of Canada approves of it. As I said, we took the first occasion open to us to acquaint the House with the question before us.
That is, the amendment.
We are discussing the same issue on the amendment of my right hon. friend, and it is just as agreeable to
me.
In other words, the Minister of Justice said: "The other day I presented a motion of confidence and asked the House to vote on that motion before we proceeded with any other business." When this amendment intervened he said: "This amendment is just the same to me as the motion which I then proposed," and he asked the House to decide 14011-10
the question before any other business was taken up. Further he says:
It is important that the issue should be settled-
When?
-at once. Public Offices must be filled-
I ask the House to note this:
-and the ordinary measures of administration must be taken, and parliament being now in session, there is no reason why the normal functions of government should not be resumed and discharged immediately.
I pause to ask this: Have the normal functions of government been suspended? If they have been suspended, then what is the reason for that suspension? Because the government, and more particularly the Prime Minister, admit that they have not the confidence of the people of this country, nor have they the confidence of this House. That is the reason it is suspended. Then my hon. friend the Minister of Justice proceeded:
We all desire the situation to be regularized, in order that we shall have a government with full moral and political authority for the tasks, domestic, imperial and international, that lie before it.
He concludes with these words:
By the verdict and the decision of my colleagues in this House of Commons I state that the government is willing to stand and will abide.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I leave the Minister of Justice and proceed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), the second most important legal adviser of this House. The Solicitor General, at page 01 of Hansard, has this to say:
Parliament in this matter must be supreme, and it is in the decision of parliament that we trust and rely. Let parliament decide the issue.
He continues:
In matters of this kind parliament is supreme and its decision will be binding. This is very plain language.
Then, towards the end of his speech, he says:
It is exactly for the purpose of getting an answer from the Progressives as to whether they are willing to support this government or whether they are not, that parliament has been called.
The Solicitor General tells this House, following the utterances of the Minister of Justice, that this matter must be decided first, that parliament has been called primarily not for the ordinary despatch of business, but for what? To decide whether or not the government shall be continued in office. Further he says:
They are absolutely free to express whatever views they think best. If they decide to support the government, we remain; if they decide not to support it, we go.
Now I call to witness a third minister, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), and



Government's Right to Office
I am done with my quotations. The Minister of the Interior, the third representative of this moribund government that we 'have in the House of Commons, says this:
The question we are to ask ourselves now is whether or not this government did the proper thing in remaining in office and in calling parliament. We have acted conscientiously within the limit of the law, and we are prepared to stand or fall by the decision which will be recorded in this House when the vote is taken.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what I ask is this: In the face of these utterances by three responsible ministers of the crown, how can my hon. friends opposite now, late in the debate, stand in their places as they have been doing, and as I understand the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) is about to do when I get through-he has been priming himself for it for the last twenty-four hours, and I see he has a good accumulation of documents on his desk-how can other members of the government and members of the government party now face the House and say, contrary to all logic, contrary to all the known precedents in the matter: if you vote against the government by supporting the amendment, you vote lack of confidence, but if you vote for the government and against the amendment, you do not express confidence in the government. Mr. Speaker, the thirg is ludicrous, it i3 absurd, and without any reason in it. It is a definite vote of confidence that the government is asking.
I ask the government now, assuming that this resolution is defeated, how are they going to stand? As they are to-day, as they have been doing, without power to function as a government? I am quoting the very words of the Minister of Justice, who declares that the government has not' been functioning in the ordinary affairs of administration; he tells the House that the government could not function until it is given a vote of confidence by the House, and now they say a vote for the government's motion is not a vote of confidence. I ask them, how are they going to function? Are they going to bring up large questions, such as the Minister of Justice referred to, and in reference to which he said the government were unable to proceed at present, or are they going to let these questions remain in abeyance? Are they going to come before this House and stand on their two feeit, or are they going to come here cringing on their knees? This is the question the House has to decide. Is this country to have a government that can hold up its head and face the people and say: We are going to administer affairs with a clear-cut mandate from the people? Or are we to have a government that will simply slip around the lobbies trying to cling to office by any

chicanery or seductive inducements they may be able to hold out here and there to members of the House, independent of all principles?
If this vote is carried in favour of the government, if the amendment is defeated, just look at the press of this country to-morrow morning. Look at the Toronto Star, look at the Montreal Herald, look at other Liberal papers throughout the country, and what will you see? Glaring headlines-Government Sustained in a Vital Vote-Liberal Government Vindicated-A New Lease of Life for the Liberal Party-and so forth. That is the kind of headings you will see in to-morrow morning's paper if the amendment is defeated. The Citizen, published in this city, will have a two-inch headline across the top of its page-

speechtext: Three inch.

speechtext:
-perhaps three inch, declaring that parliament has again expressed confidence in the government. And yet my hon. friends opposite, in order to evade or circumvent what is a legtimate conscientious doubt in the minds of some, come before parliament and suggest that a vote against the amendment is not a vote of confidence in the government!
Now let me address myself directly, and briefly, to the constitutional point. In doing this I want to make an assertion which I do not think will be disputed. The Conservative party, of which I am a member and have been for many years, the party led in this House by my right hon. friend the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meaghen), stands four-square, unflinchingly, without apology, upon the British constitutional practice. We believe, Mr. Speaker, in the institutions that have grown up under and through our constitutional growth; we believe in the sanctity of contracts, not only for the government but for the people; we believe in the inviolability of the courts of the country; we believe that parliament should function as it has functioned for so many years, as a representative body; we believe further, that a government should be a responsible government, responsible to the parliament of Canada and to the people at large. These are some of the cherished views of the Conservative party, and so I approach the constitutional question with some confidence so far as we are concerned.
I look upon the constitution as for the nation, and not the nation for the constitution. We have heard a good deal about precedent. I think, Mr. Speaker, we should be more interested in established principles growing out of

Government's Right to Office
and developed from precedent to precedent than we are in individual precedents; that is, it is by growth or the evolution from precedent to precedent that the principles of our constitution have been established'. What I want to impress upon the minds of hon. gentlemen to-day is this: that what we are discussing is that a violation of constitutional practice may become an established principle. We are not dealing with a precedent that may be lightly tossed aside, but with a vital principle of our constitution.
I want to say something further, and it is this: Principles become the rights of the people, and while this parliament may be supreme in power, while it may have the power to change this or that, there are certain things it has no light to do, and one of them is this: It has no right, even though it may have the power, to jeopardize the rights of the people in this parliament. Now I submit that this House is the trustee of those principles, and we cannot lightly or carelessly discard them. These rights, Mr Speaker, have been obtained after centuries of struggle and sacrifice; these principles have been established only after a great struggle.
Now let me ask a question: What has been this great struggle? It has, in a word, been the struggle of the rights of parliament against the encroachments of a monarch, a struggle that lasted for centuries and found its culmination about the beginning of the last century- about 1867, as a matter of fact. The encroachment of aggression of the sovereign has become obsolete; it is something we need not now fear. But while there is no fear of encroachment by the sovereign upon the rights of parliament, something else has taken the place of that encroachment, and what is it? About 1867 we finally established the principle that in the Prime Minister and his executive rested the full power of government, subject, of course, to parliament. In the Prime Minister and his executive rested the fullest measure of government which at one time rested wholly in the monarch, but which through long centuries of struggle was gradually wrested from him and placed in the hands of the Prime Minister. So to-day we have this: The Prime Minister and his executive have become the governing power in this country, as in all other countries with a constitution like ours. The power to govern, the power to determine governmental matters, rests in that body. I want the House to follow me, if I can possibly make myself clear on this point. I say again, there is no danger of aggression from the crown. The last real 14011-101
effort of aggression on the .part, of the crown was in the days of George III, when he sought to be his own Prime Minister, and one of the final acts in that drama was the bill introduced by Edmund Burke depriving George III and the crown forever of the appointment of placemen and patronage therefrom. But I am not going to indulge in any of that fine argument. What I want to say is this:	Having established, as I think I have,
that the power of government rests now with the Prime Minister and his executive, I want to point out to hon. gentlemen the danger that is there. What is the danger that threatens the people's rights to-day? Not the aggression of a monarch, but the danger of the invisible power of party organization behind the government, influencing that government in a manner detrimental to the interests of the public at large. I pause then to say this, in order to make myself perfectly clear: It makes no difference whether that party organization is Liberal, Conservative, Progressive or Labour-the point is that there rests behind the government-I care not what government it may be-an invisible, an irresponsible power which has a great influence upon the government. Now I come to the point. What is the check that the people and the people's representatives have against an unfair exercise of that pow-er by a government influenced by an invisible organization such as I have mentioned? There is one check, Mr. Speaker, and one check only. I want this point particularly to sink into the minds of hon. gentlemen in this House who look upon this question as academic and trivial. I repeat that there is one safeguard and one safeguard1 only. It is that the Prime Minister and his ministers shall meet the people's representatives in parliament.
Now let me elucidate the point. Those of us who have sat in government, or have been in party caucuses where men speak very frankly on these things, know that some measure may come up which is of peculiar interest to the group who at the time have the government under their control. What is the consideration which Sometimes prevents the bringing of Such a measure before parliament? It is the question whether or not the government, or the party, it may be, in opposition, can carry the judgment of the House and, what is of far greater importance, carry the judgment of the people-because this forum is public, not secret. That is the deterring element; that is the safeguard of a people in a free country. If you remove, that safeguard; if you interfere with it in any way, if you encroach upon it in the slightest degree,

Government's Right to Ofice
to that extent, Sir, you threaten the rights of the people; you jeopardize the interest of the public and the rights of the members of parliament as representatives of the people.
Now I go a step further. We have no Prime Minister in this House. We know that two of his ministers, Mr. Marler and Mr. Massey, though without seats in this House, are exceedingly active in the councils of the party and the government. We know that they had a hand in the drafting of the Speech from the Throne. We know that hon. gentlemen whom I see on the treasury benches today were very wrathful when they learned that Mr. Marler and Mr. Massey had1 something to do with the Speech from the Throne before they were consulted'. Where are we coming to? We have a Speech from the Throne prepared by Mr. Marler, Mr. Massey, and Mr. Mackenzie King, none of whom has a seat in the House, none of whom is before us, and we are asked to consider that Speech from the Throne with these gentlemen absent. Now I come back to where I was a moment ago.	It is not that the whole fabric of
confederation is going to be wrecked on that account. That is not the point. The point is that you are opening the door to an abuse. You are opening the door, Mr. Speaker, to an attempt to undermine the most fundamental principle of parliamentary government and the greatest safeguard of the people's rights in this country.
Mention has been made of the Baldwin-Lafontaine government. Those who are better read will correct me if I am wrong, but the last case in Canada of interference by the crown in the rights of government-I am indebted to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) for this and it is a case more to the point than any occurring in 1688 and later-was that of the Baldwin-Lafontaine administration, and as a result of that interference that government resigned and appealed to the people. It was their return that gave to the parliament of Canada the final control of its affairs and settled forever any question of encroachment by the crown upon the rights of parliament. And in this vote, which will be recorded to-night as I understand it, we the members of this House are declaring whether or not we shall open the door to a violation of that principle and to the establishment of a system which will certainly not be in the interest of the public at large. If we now vote confidence in a government whose Prime Minister and other ministers are not in the House, what is to hinder a strong party that may hereafter secure control of the popular chamber from voting "that it is un-

necessary for the Prime Minister to have a seat in the House." The Prime Minister need only say: "Oh, we have the precedent." It will be argued that in 1926 parliament functioned; the question was there debated for a week and it was decided that it w as not necessary for the Prime Minister to be in the House. It may be argued, and argued rightly, that I am drawing a fine line; but I want to point out that no nation ever lost its liberty in a night. That is not the way the rights of a people are taken from them. The liberties of this great nation of which we are so proud and which we call the Dominion of Canada are the outgrowth of centuries. Brick by brick, precedent by precedent, the fabric has been built up, and out of these precedents have come the principles of government. And I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that it will not be by some catastrophe, some overwhelming event, that this governmental institution, this parliament and all that is allied to it, will be wiped out. No, but just as we have built our constitution as it were line by line, precept by precept, here a little and there a little, just in the same manner, by taking a little away to-day and a little to-morrow, by establishing a precedent here or a precedent there, we could undermine the structure as we now have it.
I think there has been some confusion on the question of power and right. I have already made some slight reference to it, and I shall not be more than a moment in carrying my point along. I, Mr. Speaker, as an individual have the power to light a fire in this chamber, but I have no right to do it. I haye the power, the physical power, to abuse or slap one of the pages, but I have not the right to do it. This government has the power-not this government, I am wrong; it has no power; I mean a government would have with a majority of seventy such as we had in 1917. Such a government has power to barter or traffic in the liberties of the people of this country. They could do some very serious damage but they have not the right to do it. Their accession to power and the fact that they have a large majority does not establish the right to do a given thing. That is what I want to impress upon this House. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day stressed the point that parliament was supreme. He is quite correct, but is it always wise, simply because we are supreme, to deal lightly with questions which may at times be obscure, but which are nevertheless of vital importance to the future? That is what I want the House to consider at this time. I will leave that phase of the subject with one further

Government's Right to Office
observation, that when we make a decision to-day we are making a decision on a clear-cut constitutional principle-not a precedent but a principle that has been established, a principle that is in itself the only real safeguard of the people. When we vote on this question, I say, we are deciding whether or not we shall depart from that principle in this case and possibly in future cases as well.
There has been introduced into this debate, I think first by the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), an argument which I shall deal with. I hesitate, Mr. Speaker, to approach this argument, because I do not think it should ever have been obtruded into this discussion. I desire to say to my hon. friend, although some differ with me in this, that I thought he made as good an argument on his side of the case as perhaps could be made. He is a clear thinker and a forceful debater, and I congratulate him on his speech. The hon. gentleman said that the defeat of the government would place in office my right hon. friend as Prime Minister with 116 members behind him. Then, addressing himself, as the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) did, to the Progressive party and the Independents, he said that if such a thing happened we would have in office a party who stood for high tai'iff. Now that argument, that suggestion, that insinuation is not germane to the subject under discussion, but since it has been obtruded into the debate I am going to deal with it very briefly.
I think it may be stated that the Liberal party and the Progressive party are low tariff men. Anyway they are against protection; I will put it that way. On the other hand it is argued that the Conservative party are opposed by both Progressives and Liberals. We are deeply indebted to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) for some very clear-cut statements in this matter and for a good deal of help. I am not bound to argue therefore, from my own point of view only; I can enlist his assistance because he clearly stated that in the province of Quebec there were a large number who were distinctly protectionists. I could call the roll, but this is not the time to do it; I am now answering an argument. I could challenge thirty-five members on the other side of the House, yes forty-five, and not one of them would dare say that he was opposed to the general tariff policy declarations of the party to which I belong.
The point I want to bring out is that the tariff question does not constitute the whole of the policy of this party and is not the only issue. The hon. members on this side of the House, one hundred and sixteen strong, stand
without equivocation, without apology, at all times, out of the House and in the House, frankly for a reasonable protective tariff. We do not disguise our position. We do not say to any group: Well, we will meet you here, there or elsewhere on this question. The country knows where we stand. My hon. friends to my left know where we stand, and we offer no apology for our position. But when my hon. friends are asked to vote against a vital constitutional principle on the ground, forsooth, that we have a certain tariff policy, do not forget that the ranks into which you are asked to enter, that spider's web into which you are invited to enmesh yourselves, contains forty or fifty members whose tariff policy is not one whit different from ours; the only difference is that they have not the courage to stand up and say so.
Then the Solicitor General said: "The party to the left of you, Mr. Speaker, is divided; the members from Nova Scotia entered this House on a Maritime rights programme." All right, let us see whether they did or not. I hold in my hand the Sydney Post of date November 17. I will not read it at length, but I wish to quote something which will not perhaps be very acceptable to some hon. gentlemen opposite. The Sydney Post in an editorial says this:
Everyone in Nova Scotia knows that the tariff was not only the dominant issue, but that it was the sole question of serious importance discussed in this province during the recent campaign.
That is answer No. 1 to my hon. friend.

In Cape Breton island, where 90 per cent of the people are convinced protectionists, the Liberal candidates made no serious attempt to meet the Conservative arguments for a fairer tariff, but represented themselves as being quite as sturdy champions of increased protection to coal and steel as their opponents. In Cape Breton South, Mr. Currie, the Liberal candidate, professed earnestly that he stood for stiff tariff protection to local industry. In Cape Breton North and Victoria Mr. Kelly-
Mr. Kelly was the hon. member for that district in this House for four years. He was defeated by a Conservative. The editoriV continues:
Government'a Right to Office

Mr. Kelly, the King government's standard-bearer, not only claimed to be favourable to all the protection that could be procured for coal and steel, but even went so far as to criticize Mr. Meighen for not pledging himself with sufficient definiteness to an increase of the import duties on those commodities. In his nomination day speech at Port Hood, Dr. A. W. Chisholm, Liberal candidate for Inverness-
Dr. A. W. Chisholm was a member of this House for about twenty years, I think-a sturdy Liberal and protectionist.
-made much of the increased duty imposed on slack coal at the last session of parliament, and pointed to it as alleged evidence that the King government's position with respect to protection was sound. In Richmond-West Cape Breton, Mr. George W. Kyte-
Who is he? He was chief Liberal whip of the party at the time he was speaking, now a voice that is silent.
Mr. George W. Kyte sought to break the force of the Conservative protectionist campaign by affirming and reiterating, in district after district, on the platform and in his private canvass, that Mr. Meighen's vote against last year's budget was impliedly a vote against the increased duty on slack coal announced in that budget.
There are a lot of others which I will not read. The reason I interject this is to point out to hon. members the suggestions, the innuendoes, the arguments-shall I grace them with that term?-of my hon. friends opposite, to the effect that to trust a government headed by my right hon. leader would be to challenge the rights of hon. gentlemen who hold views slightly different from his.
Let me repeat what has been said already: We are not here offering policy for policy; we are not offering a quid pro quo for something offered on the other side. We stand by our principles and our policies; we stand where we have always stood-as constitutionalists, and as in favour of a reasonable tariff, but we say to the House at this time:	This
is a question that cannot be made a subject of barter. This is a question on which you cannot bid for support here or there on matters not pertaining to the question itself. We are deciding a point which is vital to the constitution and to the interests of the country. Before leaving that point, let me remind hon. members that the popular vote should rule; that the majority opinion of the people must be respected in this House. That is what we say. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and some hon. gentlemen in other sections of the House have time and again stressed the point that respect should be had for majority opinion. We entirely agree with that view. If we argue with some vigour now, if we state our views as emphatically as we can and press our arguments as strongly as we can, it
(Mr. Stevens.]
is not because we want to deprive others of a similar privilege; it is simply that we feel confident in our cause and desire to explain it to the House. What for? To get the majority opinion of this House. If the majority opinion of the country, as represented by 116 members in one part of the House and 40 or 50 in another, is that there should be a reasonable tariff, reasonable protection for agriculture and for industry, then we say that it is the right of hon. members of the House to express that opinion. That is our position in regard to the matter.
Let me say a few words as to the future. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said to us: If this amendment carries and the Conservatives are called upon to take over the affairs of the country, what are you going to do? I will say very clearly-and in this regard I know I shall carry with me the judgment of all the members who sit around me-we will religiously and rigidly follow established constitutional practice. We will respect the constitution and those principles to which I have already alluded. Shall we carry on? The question, will you carry on? has been bandied from one side of the House to the other. Let me point out that whether the government is sustained, or is defeated and a new government is called upon to take office, the constitutional duty of the administration, whichever it may be, is to carry on the affairs of the country so long as it can command a majority of the House of Commons. There is but one proviso-and it is obvious without my stating it-namely that in the case of some emergency, some great problem arising which this parliament has no mandate to deal with, unquestionably there would have to be an appeal to the people for a mandate. But on all other matters, on all questions affecting merely the carrying on of the duties of a government, this party or that party must, as a matter of duty to the people of Canada, carry on as long as it can command the support of a majority in the House of Commons.
Before I conclude, let me put this question briefly. I have asked myself for a week: Why is it that this government persists in clinging to office in face of public opinion and contrary, I know, to the advice of many of their leaders? What invisible influence is it that forces them to cling to office? I am precluded by the rules of the House from saying very much in that regard, but I will say this: It is the consciousness of this government thjjt the moment they relinquish office, the moment they surrender their seals, the moment others have access to the files and secret information of the departments, there will be revealed a

Government's Right to Office
condition which they, if they can cling to office, would fain hide.

speechtext:
In order to allay the alarm which the Minister of Finance has exhibited,
I hasten to say that I have not in mind at the moment the Minister of Finance or his department. At the earliest opportunity that is afforded, we will say more. For four years Mr. Mackenzie King-now absent from this House but still claiming the support and confidence of the House in his absence-carried on an administration that spelled failure. No one disputes that. He himself admits it. He told his electors-yes, he told all the people of Canada in his official address-that he had had for four years failed to cope with many important questions that were before the country. He declared that he had lost confidence in himself. He sought to restore that confidence by an appeal to the people and the people denied him that restoration of confidence. Now, through a petitioner, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) he comes to this House and to you, Sir, and he says: Mr. Speaker, Madam and gentlemen, if you please I have lost confidence in myself. I have sought it in the country in vain. Now, by my trusty friend, the Minister of Justice, I ask you: Tell me please, tell me, have you not that confidence in me which I have lost in myself and which the country has also lost in me?
Tile essential question, the very marrow of the problem before us, is this: The Prime Minister's presence in this House is the only evidence we can have of his submission to the constitution of this country and the authority of parliament. No Prime Minister, standing outside of the precincts of this House, refusing to face his opposition, his questioners, his critics, can claim to have submitted himself to the House. So I say that the essential thing is his presence here. Specious declarations by his henchmen and followers inside the House or outside of it will not do. He has not attempted to secure a seat in this House. Had the Prime Minister been running for a seat there might have been some force in their arguments, but up to this moment he has flouted the demands of the people and disregarded their rights. He has not even evidenced a desire to get a seat in order to be present in this House and to meet parliament. Stripped of all confusing side issues or palliatives or inducements that have been held out, the question is: Does this government properly and correctly represent the views of the majority of the people of Canada? Have they from the people such a mandate as would warrant their assuming the role of advisers of His Excellency? We say emphatically: no. We challenge that right; we challenge their action. We demand their removal; we demand the restoration of parliamentary practice and the recognition of that sacred principle to which I have alluded. We ask that we be given, by the recognition of that principle, the right and privilege of forming a ministry clothed with authority and constitutionally established.

I can safely say, however, that not one of that long line has brought to the position more tact, more patience, more urbanity and more dignity than your honourable self. Government's Right to Office

In order that there may be no misunderstanding on this point let me read the right hon. gentleman's words:
A speech from the Throne has been read, and one of them moves in this House that this Speech from the Throne be taken into consideration on a fixed date. That is a government motion. Now I contend that this House cannot, that this House certainly ought not-and I use both phrases without qualification-take into account any Speech from the Throne which comes from an alleged government through the mouth of His Excellency when that alleged government has not a prime minister in this House or in the other House answerable to parliament.
The Prime Minister writes the Speech from the Throne. I stop not to quote the authorities now; they are numerous; the Speech from the Throne is written by him or under his direction. The Speech from the Throne comes from him to this House through the mouth of His Excellency.
That is an admission that if the amendment is carried the policies which have been expounded to this country by the leader of the opposition, notably the high tariff policy which he has preached throughout Canada, will have to be embodied in a Speech from the Throne. These policies he has advocated in all parts of the country with the exception of the province of Quebec, where during the election campaign he either did not dare put in an appearance, or perhaps was prevented from so doing by those who were 5 p.m. representing themselves to bo candidates of the Conservative party under the direction of Mr. Patenaude. His high tariff policy, I say, if the present motion were defeated, would have to be embodied in a Speech from the Throne which would be put into the mouth of His Excellency the Governor General by the right hon. gentleman himself. [DOT] If the amendment now before us is carried by this House, not only must this House of Commons adjourn but it must be prorogued in order that a new session may be called; and at that new session the Governor General will have to read the Speech from the Throne submitted to him by our hon. friends opposite.

You will say: What right have you to say that? How do you know they would have voted against his policy? Because we have here the members of the Labour group, and I have heard them in this House for the past four years advocating social legislation and saying, directly and implicitly, that they are more Liberal than the Liberals; we have also in this House those members of the Progressive party who during the last session were termed perhaps by themselves and by the press of this country, perhaps unjustly, Tbs Ginger group, claiming that they were more Liberal than the other members of the Progressive party, and wc have also heard the leaders of the Pro-gicssive party themselves state time and time a mi in in this House that they were more Liberal than the members of the old Liberal party. What else could we have done? I think I have already answered the question, and if that is the case, I ask my friends of the Progressive party: Shall they condemn us for doing what we have done, shall they condemn us for having given them an opportunity to vote on the question of determining who shall rule in this country?
I do not pretend for a moment that the Liberal party of Canada constituted as it is at the present time, can carry on and rule for the next four years in this country. The Liberal party in parliament is a minority party, there is no doubt about that. We can only rule with the help and the co-operation of those who have declared on many occasions
Government's Right to Office

that they are more Liberal than we ourselves. If they are willing to co-operate with us, if they are willing to give us an opportunity, at least, of expounding our policy, if they are willing to give the members of this parliament an opportunity of discussing the merits and the demerits of the policy contained in the Speech from the Throne; if they are willing to give my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition an opportunity to propound his policy in the form of an amendment, and if they desire to compare the two, they certainly must vote against the amendment and allow us to continue with the work of the session. I have told them before it is not our intention to bind them for the future. Even if it was our intention we could not bind them. Every man in this parliament is a free agent. Every man in this parliament has the right to vote upon every measure which comes before the House; and everyone knows that, following the British constitutional practice my right hon. friend is so proud of, no party in this country could exist five minutes in opposition to the popular will, if on any important measure introduced by it, it did' not control a majority of the votes in this House. I ask, shall we have co-operation? I want, in this connection, to read for the benefit of all those within the sound of my voice, an extract from an editorial published' in the Winnipeg Free Press yesterday. It embodies my opinion-and I say this as a member of the government-as to what should be done:
The only government that has any business trying to hold office under existing conditions is one that is broadened out. to represent elements that together make up a majority. If this broadening out is impracticable for reasons good or bad, real or bogus, this parliament is a blank; and the sooner it is sent to the barn the better for the country.
We do not believe that this country wants to see Mr. Meighen in office applying his pet nostrums. A majority in parliament is certainly opposed to his policies. If this majority can unite upon a basis of reasonable compromise it can, we think, bring into being a government which will command the support both of parliament and the country.
But if this majority cannot emerge from this present confusion the country will look elsewhere for leadership. If the Liberals and the Progressives choose to look for things about which they can quarrel instead of issues upon which they can agree; if they prefer cherishing grudges to establishing friendships; if they persist in the attitude of reciprocal exclusiveness and superiority, their fate will be upon them both in a few short weeks.
With all that I most certainly agree.

There are a few other matters I wanted to discuss, but the hour is far advanced and everyone desires to reach a vote to-night. However, there is one point I would like to discuss before I take my seat; that is what my right hon. friend considers to be the main reason why this government has not the right to carry on

the absence of the right hon. Prime Minister from his seat in parliament.

speechtext:
From a seat in parliament.
I am willing to be corrected any time my hon. friend's opposite desire to correct me. Now the gist of their argument is this: Because the Prime Minister has not a seat in parliament the government has no right to carry on. I have attended many sessions of parliament where the leader of the government was absent and where some other minister conducted the affairs of the country, led the government and was the link between the government and His Majesty's representative. I am willing to *admit that if this was a permanent state of affairs and that the right hon. leader of the Liberal party had no intention of securing a seat in the House and of coming back to parliament, he would have no right and no mandate to remain as Prime Minister of Canada. And I know the question will be immediately asked; Well, why is he not here? Why did he not come back sooner? Leaving aside the musty volumes of ancient history, leaving aside the precedents and putting away from the chamber the ghosts of Pitt and Gladstone and all the others, let me use the common sense argument upon which after all British traditions and British constitution are built. The Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King was defeated in the constituency of North York in the last general election. A large number of his ministers were also defeated
in the province of Ontario. A government composed of at least eleven ministers was returned by the people, and no party in this House had an absolute majority. My right hon. friend the leader of the government could have done the same thing as the right hon. leader of the opposition did in 1921. He could have appointed someone to a position of emolument under the crown. He could have followed the example of the right hon. leader of the opposition when he appointed the hon. member for Grenville to a position in the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment department. I desire to say that I do not stand here to blame the right hon. leader of the opposition for what he did in 1921. He was defeated in that election, and he was at the head of the smallest group in the House, but he felt that, as the leader of the Conservative party, he was entitled to a seat in parliament. One of his followers was willing to give him that seat. Owing to the intricacies of the rules that hon. member could not resign, and the right hon. member took the roundabout way of opening a constituency by appointing him to a position, to make sure that the right hon. gentleman would be here when the House opened. I am not blaming him for that. I believe that the leadfers of all parties in the country should have seats in the House, and will always advocate that there should be an agreement between the parties in this House to allow their leaders to be elected in their respective seats by acclamation, in order that they may preach the gospel of their parties throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and not be confined to the sordid manipulations which may be involved in the effort to win individual seats for themselves. But my right hon. leader has a different sense, a more refined and exalted sense of honour and propriety than I have myself, and more refined than that held by the right hon. leader of the opposition. I think we agree in approving the action he took in 1921.

My right hon. leader blamed him in 1921 for what he had done. Did you expect him to do the same thing in 1925? Mr. Meighen.

But I do not think it is relevant to the issue. I think my hon. friend will know about it in the very near future, because it makes no difference whether this government is sustained or defeated, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King will have a seat in this House and will come back as leader of the Liberal party, and, whether he sits on the right or left of the Speaker, he will be elected by a handsome majority, and will have behind him the united support of every member of the Liberal party. He may lead the opposition in this parliament, but if he leads the opposition until the next general election he will be able to go to every province of Canada and preach the doctrine of the Liberal party, and will not be obliged to engage anybody else to preach his policy by proxy.
I desire to refer to the absence of my right hon. leader from the House. Everyone knows, reading through all the British precedents, that ministers have often occupied seats in the cabinet of a nation without, for a certain time, being members of parliament. We all know my right hon. leader intends to come back to parliament at the earliest possible moment. We all know it is not owing to the absence of offers of safe seats that he did not return, and for that reason I do not think his absence an argument which would justify even my Progressive friends in voting for the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition. I admire my right hon. leader for the stand he has taken. I admire him not only for not having imposed himself as Prime Minister of this country, but for not even having attempted to impose himself as the leader of the Liberal party. When the members of the Liberal party, coming from every province of this great and' broad Dominion, met here at Ottawa in caucus on the first occasion, their very first act, without hesitation of any kind, was to express unanimously a vote of confidence in the great leader of the Liberal party. It is true that our leader was defeated. It is not the first time that a political leader has suffered defeat. It is not the first time that the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King has suffered defeat. But there are three kinds of leaders. There are those who having been defeated once, have remained defeated

Government's Right to Office
and fallen; there are those who are carried in on the crest of the wave and there are those who are able to suffer defeat and who come back again and win their laurels. That is what the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King has always done and will do. It is true that he was defeated. His defeat, however, was not due to any personal conduct of his own, nor to the fact that he was unworthy of sitting for the constituency of North York. He was defeated on a policy which did not appeal to the majority of the people of Ontario at that particular time. That is why he wrent down to defeat.

I do not know that
any pledges made by the Prime Minister were broken. I do not think my hon. friends on the other side will be able to claim that many of his pledges were broken. If he was not elected, it was because the people of the constituency of North York agreed with the high protective tariff policy preached by my right hon. friend. But I would prefer to follow a leader who has preached throughout the length and breadth of Canada the same programme and the same policy.
