subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
There are laughs of derision from my hon. friends on the other side; but I happen to know whereof I speak, because I accompanied the Prime Minister in five provinces of this great Dominion in this last campaign, and I can truthfully say, upon my honour as a member of this House, that in every one of those five provinces he preached -the same policy. He preached the policy of broad Canadianiam. He went to the western prairies and told- the farmers there that undoubtedly they would be obliged to make certain concessions to the industrial centres in the east. Coming east to Ontario and Quebec, where I heard him twice in my own old province, he preached the same doctrine, telling the industrial population -of Quebec that -they must also make concessions to the farmers who had gone out to till the soil in the wrestern prairies. He told them that Quebec was not all Canada; that Ontario was not all Canada; that they must also consider the western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and- Alberta as part of our Dominion, as well as British Columbia and -the Maritime -provinces; -that the policy to be enunciated, promulgated here by the
Liberal party-it would apply to the Progressive party, because I know on many points there is no difference-that the policy to be enunciated here by the government, which must have and which, I am sure, will have the support of the Progressive members of this House, must be a broad Canadian policy containing concessions to every province, respect for the rights of all the provinces, and encouraging the farmer of western Canada and the workman of the province of Quebec -to work hand in band and shoulder to shoulder for the welfare of our great and common country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. CHARLES H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):	I come to -this House, Mr. Speaker, as a new member. Some thirty-seven or thirty-eight years ago I did belong to the fourth estate and I sat at that time in the press gallery where I listened to and reported the speeches of distinguished statesmen; but apart from that, and some service as leader of the Conservative party in my own native province in the legislature, my political experience in parliament is limited indeed.
My first duty and my great pleasure is, in the most sincere manner possible, to congratulate you, Sir, upon- your re-election to the important office which you now fill. For yourself, Sir, as you well know, I have had for m-any years a warm personal esteem and, I might also say, a persona! affection; and although you and I were opposing candidates in a constituency in a great crisis in the history of Canada, and though we both spoke our minds with the utmost frankness, I th-ink I can say that when the contest ended the mutual personal esteem between you, the victor, and myself, the vanquished, had- been increased by the very conflict in which we had been engaged.
It seems to me, Sir, that this debate has been confused somewhat -by reason of the fact that we have not gone back to elementary principles. What is constitutional practice and what are constitutional precepts? And if they are not to be obeyed and followed, what are -the penalties which parliament and the country suffer by the refusal to follow those precepts? I am going back to the very first page of Todd on Parliamentary Government in England in which it is stated:
The government of England is conducted in conformity with certain traditional maxims, which limit

Government's Right to Office
the exercise of all political powers therein. These maxims are, for the most part, unwritten and conventional. They have never been declared in any formal charter or statute, but have developed, in the course of centuries, side by side with the written law. They embody the matured experience of successive generations of statesmen in the conduct of public affairs, and are known as the precepts of the constitution.
And further, on the following page:
It is the distinguishing feature of parliamentary government that it requires the powers 'belonging to the crown to be exercised through ministers, who are held responsible for the manner in which they are used, who are expected to be members of the two houses of parliament, the proceedings of which they must be able generally to guide, and who are considered entitled to hold their offices only while they possess the confidence of parliament, and more especially of the House of Commons.
These are the precepts embodying the wisdom and experience of the men who have guided the affairs of England through preceding generations, and when we depart from these precepts we invite into the administration of our public affairs evils of a very serious character which imperil the civil liberties of the people.
I have had some experience, Sir, in the republics south of the Rio Grande river where they have adopted, by way of code, what they regard as the precepits of British constitutional practice. The president of the republic usually has, in the exercise of his functions, similar duties and responsibilities to those of the Prime Minister of this country, and in their elections it is alleged that they follow in form the British constitutional practice. But in that practice the men opposing each other and playing what they call the parliamentary game are in honour bound to conduct the contests and abide by their results according to the rules which govern such contests in Great Britain and the British dominions. In the south they occasionally, and perhaps not infrequently, refuse to follow these precedents and precepits, with this result:	I
have Mime and time again seen an election in which the president and his party, having gone to the polls, failed to receive a majority of the votes, and, refusing to abide iby the precepits which would compel him to surrender the administration to the opposing party, the president has endeavoured to continue in office. I have noticed, as you will find if you study the political history of those republics, that there are three means by which he endeavours to avoid compliance with the decision given by the people at the polls. The first is by attempts frequently made to bribe those who have been elected to oppose him, and thus nullify to that extent the public verdict. The second, when bribery fails, is to use intimidation in order to thwart

the public verdict. When that, fails, only one other course is left to him, and frequently he appeals to physical brute force-military force -to keep himself in office. The events of which you read in the newspapers from day to day and from month to month with regard to these various revolutions in the republics south of the Rio Grande river are due to the fact that the administration, defeated at the polls, refuses to abide by the verdict of the people and by those constitutional precepts which have been adopted for the carrying on of the game of political warfare, and uses one of the three means which I have suggested to remain in office. I take the responsibility, although a new member, of suggesting to this House that if the government of to-day or the government of any future day refuse to abide by these precepts governing parliamentary conduct, governing the relations of the parties in a general contest foy public support, there are only three means by which they may be kept in office if the verdict is against them. That is, by bribery of those elected to oppose them, or by intimidation if bribery does not succeed-and when those two means fail we are on the eve of a revolution. Those are the evils which are induced by a refusal to abide by the precepts which govern these contests.
Following the recent election we have this result: The Prime Minister stated deliberately to the people of the whole country, speaking at Richmond Hill, that although his parliamentary term had not expired he found it absolutely impossible to carry on an efficient administration; he found it absolutely impossible to solve the economic, fiscal and financial problems which beset this country, and in order that he might have a majority sufficient to solve those problems and to give stable government, he declared that he was appealing to the people to give him a majority in excess of that majority of one which he then held over Conservatives and Progressives combined. If I understand what he said, he intimated that if he did not secure more than a majority of one over those elected as Conservatives, those elected as Progressives. _ those elected as representing Labour, and those elected as Independents, from his experience of the last four years it would be impossible for him to carry on an efficient administration. I heard the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) who spoke before me, refer again and again to the Jfine sense of honour and propriety of the late Prime Minister of this country. I ask, Mr. Speaker, even the Liberals who sit opposite me, whether in view of that pledge the Prime Minister can be commended upon his fine

Government's Right to Office
sense of honour and propriety in refusing to abide by the decision of the electors which he himself invited.
I am not going into the authorities, although I have taken the trouble, with such measure of strength as I have, to examine those authorities cited on both sides. My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), whose legal acumen and industry in research I have often admired-and I may say I do admire him except for the few eccentricities which he shows on the public platform at election time-has searched out every precedent which could be cited on the government side, and both those precedents simply apply to the case where, during a session of parliament, a minister has accepted office under the crown and has gone to seek immediate election-as he, is bound to do-in order that he might have the approval and confirmation of his constituency, to enable him to hold that office. But apart from that it is not, I am sure, in accordance with the recognized customs, precepts, practice and procedure of parliamentary government, or with the spirit which pervades our parliamentary institutions, that parliament should convene after a general election for the despatch of public business without having the Prime Minister of the country sitting in his seat to announce his policy, and to act as the sole intermediary between this parliament and the Governor General representing the crown. This is especially true in view of the fact that eight of his ministers have been defeated at the polls, not one of whom has since sought or obtained the confidence of the electors of a constituency, and that the Prime Minister has come to parliament with an Address from the crown, placed-and I use the word with great deference-upon the lips of His Excellency the Governor General by a defeated leader and prepared, as has been practically announced, by two ministers, with the Prime Minister, who have not been able to obtain the confidence of their constituents in their recent appeal in the general election.
There are matters in that Speech which, if I were called upon to identify them with as much precision as one could identify the handwriting of a friend, I think I could point out as having been provided by my recent opponent in St. Lawrence-St. George. It is indeed, as Mr. Morley has said, a political anomaly which should not be tolerated, that after a general appeal to the constituents there should be submitted to parliament a political programme prepared by a former Prime Minister and former ministers of his appointment who are no longer members of or personally 14011-it
responsible to parliament for the due performance of their duties as part of the executive. Particularly is this the case when there is presented to parliament a programme differing in almost every essential from that on which hon. gentlemen made their recent appeal to the electors of this country. There can be no doubt, I think, as to the soundness of my contention, and if I had the strength and the time I would like to go through precedent after precedent and authority after authority in support of my proposition. There can be no doubt, I think, that, in the words of the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition, their attempted continuance in office is a violation of the principles and practice of British constitutional government. It is not only a violation of the principles and precepts and practice of British constitutional government; it is more than that. It is a moral delinquency in that, as admitted by speaker after speaker, and especially by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) who spoke this afternoon, the Speech was prepared and intended, as a South American autocrat might so prepare and so intend it, to induce, if I am at liberty in the house of parliament ,to say so, the members of the Progressive group, by corrupt inducements-

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
I withdraw the remark, Mr. Speaker. I will see if I can put it in parliamentary language. Mr. Speaker, I regard certain paragraphs of that Speech prepared by the leader of the government and his colleagues as an effort to obtain the support of members of the Progressive group, who were elected to oppose him, by offering to them as a group and as a class special inducements which he did not dare offer when the general elections *were on-a time when any such offer or inducements would necessarily be presented not only to the gentlemen who form the Progressive group, but to the electors of the entire country, so that the whole country could pass upon them.
I have been humiliated, as a new member of the House of Commons, to hear this talk of bids, of valises or bags full of bids offered to this special group of the Progressives. Sir. I do not know the Progressive members. I have not had the pleasure of meeting them

Government's Right to Office

and of their acquaintance, but I hope under ithe present circumstances it may not be said that any member of the Conservative party offers to them inducements or gifts, similar to those which have been offered in the Speech of His Excellency the Governor General. More than that, Sir, the very presence in the Speech of His Excellency of those paragraphs is a reflection not only upon the government but upon the parliament to (which they have been submitted.
I have heard from the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) some criticism of the financial interests, the money powers, so-called, of the cities of Montreal and Toronto. 1 represent one of the central districts of the pity and island of Montreal, and I can say this, stating here what I have said elsewhere: that so far as I know the will of my constituents, it is that to the utmost of my intelligence and of my application and assiduity I should apply myself to studying two sets of grievances which are now before this country; one the set of grievances which has been prepared by my native province of Nova Scotia for which I must always have the strongest possible personal affection, and the other that we should examine to the utmost of our power into every legitimate grievance presented by the west, because the city of Montreal which stands at the head of ocean navigation is much interested in the continued and increased prosperity of the three great provinces of the middle west. The prosperity of the island of Montreal depends to a large extent upon their prosperity, and there is every disposition to meet their legitimate view's presented to parliament in the proper manner and deal with them in a manner consistent with the we! being, the general interest and the general prosperity of the whole country.
Public opinion throughout Canada has been directed to the offer made to these gentlemen in the Speech from the Throne. Public opinion will condemn, I have no doubt in due time, the government which has so far departed from the platform which it submitted at the general election as to present inducements of that character to hon. gentlemen of the Progressive group. But I put it to them also that they stand to-day as the Progressive group never stood before, in the clear, concentrated light of the public opinion of this country, and the whole of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific is watching the Progressive group to know whether such inducements as those, presented under such circumstances and conditions find cordial reception from the gentlemen to whom the offer
[Mr. Cahan.l
has been made. And if these gentlemen of the Progressive group, instead of depending upon the cordial good will of the people of the whole country-because we are all Canadians from end to end with a general interest in view-if instead of depending on their own intellectual and oratorical resources in presenting their cause to this House and to the whole country, show that they are prepared to accept an indirect offer of that character, the general estimation of the Progressive group will, I believe, sink to a very low level in the Canadian public mind. That is the issue. The Progressive group do not stand here to-day as judges.

As a representative of
Montreal would you be willing to have the rate on the Canadian National from a point north of Fort William to the city of Quebec, which is about double the present prairie rate, reduced?

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
I can frankly, say to my
hon. friend that I do not know enough about the question to give him an answer, but I am prepared to sit down with him, or any other representative in this House who says he has a grievance, and listen to the facts, and if I can assist him in securing the proper solution of his difficulties and his problems I am prepared to do that so long as in doing so I do not have to sacrifice the general interests of the whole country.
I have-I think in parliamentary language since I have been corrected and since I have made due apology-indicated to these hon. gentlemen the result of making ill-considered and hasty departures from the constitutional precepts which the wisdom of statesmen has developed through successive centuries, and I have not only pointed out by analogy what occurred in the neighbouring republic south of the Rio Grande river but I have called attention to the unprecedented condition which now prevails in this country when an offer of that kind is made after a general election and as an afterthought to secure political support. I have shown them, as I think, hon. gentlemen can deduce for themselves, what evils may result and are resulting in this very case from the departure from the constitutional precepts and practice of Great Britain and Canada.
Now, the hon. gentleman who preceded me has declared that if this amendment passes a dissolution of this parliament is necessary and inevitable. Is that expressing the argument too strongly? I say that that statement, made by the hon. Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) is entirely unwarranted, is

Government's Right to Office
entirely without authority, and could be confuted by any two year old student in constitutional practice in any university in this country. What is a Speech from the Throne of which we heard so much this afternoon. A Speech from the Throne, the Address of the Governor General representing His Majesty, is a presentation to the House of the views, dispositions and purposes of the Prime Minister of the day and of his colleagues. In this case it is before the House and recorded upon the records and with respect to it the sole duty, of the Commons in reply, if there is any duty is to note that it has received that Speech. The House might in its reply simply say by a note that it has received the Speech without any comment whatever; but the nature of that reply is entirely in the control and discretion of hon. members and not in the control or in the discretion of the members of the cabinet. Supposing the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition passes to-night. Then you have it stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) less clearly stated by the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) stated also by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), and also reiterated in a somewhat equivocal manner by the Minister of Customs and Excise this afternoon that in the event of that amendment passing the Right Hon. Mackenzie King would resign and leave the Governor General free to call upon another, whose selection is always in the discretion of the Governor Generail, so long as he commands or is likely to command a majority in the House to form a new government.	'
Now, let us see what the procedure is, because it is very, very simple indeed, and there is no need for confusion in this matter. The hon. leader of the opposition is called upon to form an administration. He selects from members in the House, or bom those who do not represent constituencies, those who are to compose his ministry, and those selected must find immediately, or a'most immediately, the constituencies which they may contest, where they may secure that confirmation which is necessary to allow a minister of the crown holding a portfolio to continue in office. Now an adjournment is always conceded for that purpose. Take the case which happened in 1924, which I remember well, when Mir. Stanley Baldwin met the House on January 8, 1924. The king's speech was delivered on January 15, 1924. A vote of want of confidence was moved and passed, and on the 22nd January Ramsay MacDonald was called upon to form a government. His first act, which is never refused under Such 14011-111
circumstances, was to ask for an adjournment of three weeks, in order that his new ministers might secure constituencies, and that he might attend to some matters of routine, necessitating the attention of the government especially, in dealing with foreign affairs, but when they met again Ramsay MacDonald did not-and so stated in the House-regard himself as bound by the terms of the Speech which had been presented. He declared that he felt himself perfectly free to carve out of it some of the things of which he approved, to entirely disregard other things of which he did not approve, and to deal with other important measures which he mentioned, which had the approval of the Labour party, and which had been embodied in the Labour platform, and to deal with those without regard to the king's message. I am saying this without the slightest fear of contradiction by any man who has looked into the precedents and the facts. Let us take this case: the right hon. leader of the opposition is called upon to form an administration and does so; he asks for an adjournment, to which he is entitled, for three or four weeks, or the time necessary for his ministers to seek re-election. He comes back to this House with his ministers re-elected, and he simply finds the Speech from the Throne as a matter of unfinished business on the records of this House. The reply of this House to that Speech from the Throne, which has been made the order of business, is entirely within the discretion of the majority of the members of this House. They may disregard entirely in their reply every single paragraph of that Speech, or they may adopt certain paragraphs, and in the Address in reply represent to His Majesty that they no longer agree to nor intend to carry out the policy announced by their predecessors.

No, I am out of the hospital ten days only, after a long illness; I am very weak and tired to-night, and I do not think it is necessary that I should go into all these irrelevant matters. If any hon. gentleman has any doubt as to how the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne may be presented in one form, and then subjected* to amendment after amendment, until every phase of opinion represented by every two members of the House who can move and second a resolution may be brought before the House for consideration, then I invite him to consider the proceedings in the House of Commons of the 13th and 14th March, 1894. I have them before me and intended to go into them to-night, but I am too fatigued to do it. Hon. members will find* that an Ad-,dress in reply to the Speech from the Throne was presented. Certain amendments were moved by private members of the House. One -was accepted and then another further amendment to the reply as so amended. Other amendments were 'brought in, amendment after amendment, and so on, until the finally revised reply came down for the consideration of the House and1 was dealt with by the House. In dealing with those matters the House of Commons is paramount. Every hon. member of this House who can secure a seconder has a right to place his individual and particular views in the shape of a resolution by way of an amendment before the House for its full consideration. It is puerile and nonsensical to suggest that the mere fact of the passing of this amendment necessitates a dissolution of the House. I have, Mr. Speaker, under my hand a large number of authorities showing that in the colonial governments the dissolution of the House is a matter in the discretion of the Governor General of this Dominion. In respect of such a dissolution he must have the advice and support of his advisers for the time being or the support of the new advisers whom he selects to form a government. I do not intend to go into that. A departure has been attempted from the precepts and practice which we are bound to follow in order to preserve the rights of this parliament, of this House of Commons and

the civil liberties of the subjects of His Majesty throughout the Dominion. We see, from the nature of the discussion which has taken place with respect to certain inducements offered to a special group in this House, the evils which are resulting and will result from a departure from well-established precept and principle. If you go beyond that you come to the point where nothing but bribery or brute force will enable the representatives of a majority to maintain their right to enter upon the administration of the country whenever an autocrat of the type of Mussolini or Pangalos of Greece endeavours to override and subvert parliamentary institutions. The people are beginning to believe that parliamentary institutions, as we here are administering them, are subversive of the very best interests of the country. I make no special appeal to the Progressives. I make no special appeal to any group in this House. We are all Canadians representing Canadian interests and anxious to promote the development and well-being and to safeguard the interests of the whole country, and through you, Sir, I appeal to hon. members of this House, elected by Canadian constituencies, to vote for this amendment in order to crush the head of the autocratic and despotic form of government which my hon. friends opposite are attempting to introduce into the parliamentary institutions of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have now for about a week been discussing what I imagine to be one of the greatest and most momentous issues that have ever arisen in this House-an issue in which is bound up the present and the future practice of parliament; an issue which concerns itself and is concerned with the constitutional procedure under which governments may administer the affaire 9 p.m. of the nation; an issue which contains within itself the essence of parliamentary usage. Upon the deciding of that issue will rest the ability of parliament to function as a parliament. Because we are discussing an issue so vast in its import as far to outweigh any considerations of party welfare, any considerations as to whether confidence may well be reposed in one set of men or another set of men, an issue so important that beside it even the immediate policy of this country will fade into pallid insignificance, I propose to deal-and not from any angle of policies or governments or .parties-with the specific case that is before us. I propose to deal with it, as far as possible, without the slightest feeling of partisanship; and I can the more readily do that because I am a

Government's Right to Office
Progressive, a farmer, a member of the United Farmers of Alberta, unconnected with either of the old parties. To me no interest is at stake, no party consideration is involved. I care not at all which party is in power as regards this issue. Dealing as the issue does with constitutional practice, it is perhaps ironical, to say the least, that the final settlement of it, the hand which will write into the pages of our constitutional history a new precedent, will be the hand of farmers, men unversed' in the subtleties of legal lore, men largely unacquainted with the intricacies of constitutional precedent or practice. We can therefore bring to this discussion only one factor-and I believe that factor to be one of primary importance-namely, the use of our own common sense, untrammelled by partisan ties. I mention this in view of this singular fact-at least it appears singular to me. This is a question which, I say, should not, cannot be considered from the viewpoint of any party, so transcendent in importance is it to the policies of all parties.
Now, we upon whom the responsibility is thrust, through the peculiar circumstances of the case, of making the decision on this issue, find-on a subject which might well engage the considered attention of any man; which might well call for the expression of men's individual opinions-an absolute and complete unanimity amonigst 116 members of the House on one side of the case and an absolute and complete unanimity amongst 101 members on the other side of the case. In view of that fact, am I to conclude that this discussion or the consideration of this issue has been wholly free from partisanship? I have stated that I propose to discuss it, inadequate though my effort may be, on its merits. I do not, therefore, propose to discuss the Speech from the Throne. I do not, therefore, propose to discuss or consider preelection statements, foolish or wise, made by any public man. I do not propose to discuss the question whether we in this comer of the House have confidence in the actions and policies pr inactions and lack of policies of the Liberal party. I do not propose to discuss whether we have confidence in the Conservative party or in the policies which they state they intend to put into force. I propose to deal with the matter purely and simply from the viewpoint of constitutional practice as it appears to me and from the viewpoint of how parliament can more effectively function under unprecedented conditions.
As I understand the situation, exception is being taken to the action of the government- and for the purpose of my argument I am
speaking of the government now-in view of the condition of affairs existing in this country at the conclusion of the last election, in retaining office and submitting to parliament a Speech from the Throne. In other words, the question is whether their duty, when the results of the election were known, was to tender their resignation to His Excellency and advise him to call into consultation the leader of the opposition, or to meet parliament, as in fact they have done. Now what is involved in the present situation? Because much is involved; and from our point of view in this corner more is involved than from the point of view of either of the two old parties that took part in the contest. No thinking member of this House can ignore the fact that, theories apart, likes or dislikes, tastes or distastes left out of consideration, the party system as we have had it is, not now functioning. Certain conditions have introduced themselves into the public life of the country and into parliament as representing that public life which have had no parallel in our history, so far as we can escertain. Through the multiplicity of groups which have developed in this country and which are finding expression for their various points of view in the House, that condition has become inevitable.
I have listened day after day to the arguments advanced on both sides of the House by men capable of reasoning on the subject, and I have endeavoured to sift the wheat from the Chaff. With this object in view I have forgotten party arguments and have ignored the insinuations as to one side or the other having been guilty of corrupt practices or incorrect statements in the election. These things I have set aside, and I have rather endeavoured, through careful attention to the debate and a zealous reading of Hansard, to ascertain what sound parliamentary principle has been brought forward and submitted to the House. I have sou^lit to glean from the observations of hon. gentlemen who have taken part in the debate what either side of the House has had to offer in this direction, and I must confess that I have found some difficulty in doing so. And I have experienced that difficulty for this reason: that while the precedents which have been evoked are no doubt sound in themselves, the trouble is that we are now trying to apply precedents to an unprecedented condition. I do not think we can very well demonstrate the applicability of those precedents to the condition which we find here to-day; so that in this respect I have been somewhat at a loss. I have found moreover, that the disputants, even on the same side, have not always agreed
Government's Right to Office

in their interpretation of the precedents, as to the weight that should be attached to them, or as to their applicability to the present situation. It has been generally said on this side of the House that the government at present in power or at any rate the government that met defeat, in some degree at least, at the last election had no constitutional right to present to parliament the Speech which His Excellency read at the opening of the session. On the other hand, I read the opinion of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), than whom perhaps no more able exponent of parliamentary usage is to be found in this House. And what did he say? I quote:	[DOT]
The ordinary and well established course which the government should have followed-
That is, this government in the present situation.
-was to meet the House, as they did, bring in the Address, as they did, and move for the consideration of that Address on a fixed day.
So that we find the hon. member taking issue with his colleagues on this side of the House as to the constitutional nature of the action which the government should have taken. He further states that had it not been for an irregular action on the part of the government in attempting to introduce a motion which should not have been introduced, this amendment we are now discussing would not have been moved. He said that if the course he suggested had been followed the discussion of the Speech from the Throne would have taken place in due course and the House would have expressed its opinion upon it, while the Conservative opposition would have had an opportunity to state its views in the form of an amendment, so that the House as a whole might be able to judge the situation on a vote.
I cannot lightly set aside the opinion of the hon. member for South Wellington. But let us go a little further and see what the motion itself really means. It begins by Stating certain facts which are so obvious and well known to every member of this House as to call for no repetition, the facts in connection with the results following the election. On the basis of those facts the motion asserts that the government is acting unconstitutionally in bringing in the Speech which has been submitted to us. Amongst the facts so cited we find, first, that the government was defeated in the majority of constituencies, and secondly that it does not now amongst its members comprise the largest group in the House. It is stated in the third place that the Prime Minister and other members of the government are without seats in' the House.

Now, if the amendment is supported by a vote of the House what will this involve so far as the future of parliament is concerned? It will establish this prnoiple, that under all simitar circumstances, that is to say, when a government after an appeal to the people comes back in a minority, then the largest group, irrespective of the proportion which it may bear to the toral number of members in the House, shall automatically assume the reins of power and the responsibility for summoning parliament. That is what it means.
Frankly, I see two dangers in that suggestion. The first is one which perhaps may be of little weight; it may be a mere figment of my own imagination, due possibly to a lack of knowledge. As I understand the constitutional practice, His Majesty or His Majesty's representative, by and with the advice of the ministers of the crown, performs certain functions. In other words, by and with the advice of the ministers of the crown he selects and calls into council a certain man representing a certain party and asks him to form a government. But if we establish it as a maxim that automatically the largest group in the House, irrespective of the disproportion it may bear to the whole assembly, shall automatically become the recipient of the power and honours of government, then what is to become of the theory which we have held, that the Governor General, by and with the advice of the ministers of the crown, shall exercise his discretion in the circumstances ensuing from an election? That may be regarded as an insignificant point, but it is one that appeals to me as having some weight. The great danger I see in the suggestion is one that strikes the members in this comer of the House with peculiar force. We believe both in theory and as a matter of fact that the time is past when we shall have in this House and in the country two well defined parties one of which will at all times have a majority in parliament. It would be better therefore for the country under these circumstances if some form of group co-operation could be instituted. We believe that the group system will persist, and that future governments must function on a basis of co-operation among the different bodies comprising the House. That perhaps is generally but a theory. But all theories, whether they be held by a large party or only by a minor group, must some time come face to face with the granite rook of fact3, and if they cannot adapt themselves to those facts they will be shattered. The facts are apparent, and for the present at least the principle is in operation: no party in this

Government's Right to Office
House can function at this time save as part of a co-operative body.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the danger I foresee from a constitutional standpoint is that if we by our vote in this House establish as a fixed and determined principle that the larger group,-no matter whether or not they carry a majority in the House,-shall at all times be given the right to form a government, what becomes of the possibility of our opinions on present-day facts being carried into effect? I am not competent, nor do I intend, to speak of the opinions that have been expressed and the different precedents that have been [DOT]laid down for the last eighty years, let alone go back to the seventeenth or eighteenth century. I do say, however, that the British constitution has been built up by precedent after precedent-such precedent as we shall set to-day; that in the manner in which that constitution has been built up, (precedent by precedent, lies its strength, its grandeur and its adaptability. And that constitution is petrified if we take the position now that it has reached its culmination, that no change can be made, no alteration brought into effect to meet conditions which are changing. If we take that attitude we are repudiating the great- basic principle on which the British constitution itself has been founded. I am not speaking as one who has no regard for the British constitution. I am speaking as one who is British-born-a Canadian now, but British-born of British stock. I honour and respect those traditions. Never would I willingly see removed one milestone which marks our progress. I like to feel always that step by step we are linked to the Mother of Parliaments and to the time when that parliament originated; I would like to see that tradition kept in remembrance. But I would also like to see preserved that virile spirit which animates the British constitution.
I shall now pass to another point of view, the other great issue which is facing us-the ability of (parliament itself to function. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that whatever other views we hold, we maintain always the opinion that the essential duty and responsibility of parliament is to function, to carry on; that the essential duty of government is to govern. The essential duty of parliament must be to carry on, to enunciate policies, to embody those policies in legislation. In other words, unless parliament functions all theories go by the board. What is the position to-day? As I have said-and I can state it without fear of contradiction-at the present moment the party system as such cannot function. That statement may be
challenged, but it cannot be challenged successfully. The essence of the spirit of our party system is that one party or another may receive such a mandate from the country as will entitle it to bring forward a programme and command such parliamentary support within itself as will enable it to put that programme into effect. Can any party here do that to-day? Can we suggest that in future the difficulty will decrease, that in future parliaments this situation will never again occur? Hon. members may express a contrary opinion; my opinion is that the difficulty is likely to become accentuated' in the future rather than diminished. We are facing the question now: under what circumstances can parliament function, and on what basis can the government govern to-day? Obviously on one basis alone, that of co-operation between one or other of the major parties, and at least some individuals, if not entire groups, outside of that party. That fact is so obvious that it need not be stressed. Upon what basis, then, may that co-operation be brought about? On a party basis? That is impossible, because there is no party affiliation. On one basis only can parliament function-the basis of policy and legislation. Suppose for one moment this amendment carried and in due course the Conservative party took office and brought in a programme. Although that programme emanated solely from the caucus room of their own party or from the brains contained within their own party, not one jot, not one tittle of that programme could go through this House without co-operative action by other members. Everyone knows that. Hon. members on this side of the House who have spoken have admitted it.	_
Now I say again, on what basis can cooperative action be taken, can parliament function and a government administer national affairs except on a basis of legislation? In voting for this amendment what do I say? That we decide now what government shall function; that we decide now who shall take power, prior to the discussion of the very basis upon, which that government itself can function and upon which parliament can carry on. I hope I am making myself distinctly understood. I say now that I intend to vote against the amendment, just as I would have voted against the motion introduced by the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Lapointe), because in either case it would have prevented this House from functioning; it would have prevented the discussion of the very basis upon which parliament can operate. I for one was glad when the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) made his statement.
Government's Right to Office

not because I am in the habit of allowing other men to interpret my vote or my motives for me; not because I have been in the habit of placing much emphasis upon the headlines in our daily press to which reference has been made. I have usually, rightly or wrongly, made up my own mind and placed my own interpretation upon my actions, responsible only to the people whom I represent. I would not like it to be understood by the members of the government sitting across the House that by this vote I register confidence in their actions during the last four years. I make it very definite and very clear that on this question I would not be prepared to vote confidence in the government. Nor would I be prepared to vote confidence in the Conservative party. And why do I lack that confidence? Well, Mr. Speaker, it is for a most curious reason. I would be afraid, from the history of the past, that the government of the day would not put their platform into effect; and I would be afraid, from the declarations of the past, that the Conservative party would. Holding the opinions which I hold, opinions on policy and opinions on governments, which I have expressed from time to time, can any hon. member blame me for the attitude of doubt which I assume?
I have made it abundantly clear, I think, that I am not now voting confidence or lack of confidence. I am voting simply and solely on two points: first, whether under the conditions prevailing the government were justified in appealing to parliament to settle the question-and I believe they were; second, to give myself the opportunity to discuss the basis upon which we may be able to function in this House, and to pass my final decision upon policies; to follow the course that the hon. member for South Wellington said should be followed, that we may have before us the proposals of policy emanating from the Liberal party and the suggestions as to policies emanating from the Conservative party, vote on the merits of those two policies and decide which policy we can support. It is not a question of supporting this party or that, but a question of sound legislation.
I was glad for another reason to hear the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) make the statement he did, for we in this comer of the House have contended for years for the introduction of this great factor into our parliamentary life; that when we vote on an issue we should vote solely on the merits of that oarticular question without considering political implications. We endeavoured four years ago to bring about that state of affairs in this House. We moved and supported a

proposal that every legislative question should be voted on upon its merits, without party bias, and that a government should be defeated only on a direct want of confidence vote. That proposal was repudiated on both sides of the House, and now what do we find? We find that the germ of that suggestion has been accepted by the government; for we have the statement of the Minister of Customs that no implication is to be attached to a vote save as deciding the merits of the question itself.
May I say this, Mr. Speaker, I have gone through this country during the election, because I had to run an election too, and in all parts of the country in which I have gone I have found one opinion prevailing-it prevails throughout all Canada to-day, so far as I know-and that is the country is tired of politics and wants us to consider the matters that come before us as matters of business. It desires, for instance, that the great question of our trade relations as embodied in a protective policy or in a free trade policy shall be considered as a business problem, not as a political issue; that the question of transportation shall be considered in the light in which it really stands, as a business problem, capable of being settled on business lines by business men, and not as a question to be bandied from side to side as a political issue; that the questions of taxation, of credit, and all the other various problems shall be dealt with and settled as business problems, and not treated as political measures. I say that tonight we find here the germ of that idea.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, limiting my vote to the matter before the House, and leaving myself free to support sound policies and to vote against unsound policies, from whichever side they emanate, I shall vote against the amendment. In so speaking I am speaking for myself, but I believe I am also expressing the views of many in this corner of the House who will vote as I vote.

Mr. Speaker, although the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Caban) is not in his seat at the moment, I want to extend to him my most hearty congratulations upon his recovery from the severe illness which he has recently suffered. I should like to express my persona! satisfaction in seeing that he has lost none of his old vigour of previous days despite his illness. I am glad to see such a man in this House, although I do not agree with all the principles which he has laid down or with all the ideas which he has expressed, I am pleased to admit the sincerity of his motives and his very firm convictions.

Government's Right to Office
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George complained) very bitterly about what he called the bribes made by the present government for the support of the Progressive party in the vote which is to be taken before very long. I would ask him to apply the severe judgment which he has brought against the proposals contained in the Speech from the Throne to the promise of co-operation, good-will, and common understanding which have been extended from the opposite side of the House towards the Progressives in order to get their support and their votes.
The very distinguished member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), in the course of his remarks, complained because during the last three or four years the government had not been very strong and had had to get support from other parts of the House, and he said this had placed the government in a very embarrassing and humiliating position, but at the end of his speech he made an appeal for the support of these very gentlemen who had been supporting the Liberal party for the last three or four years. After blaming indirectly, if not directly, the present government for having tried to get Progressive support during the last three or four years, he expressed his desire to see the Progressive members give similar support to the party to which he belongs. At the end of his speech he was no longer afraid of the embarrassing and humiliating position in which he would be placed in having to comply with the requests of members of the Progressive group. This shows, Mr. Speaker-I d)o not want to cast any reflections upon hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House-that their first intention, their chief desire, is not to have the will of the majority prevail in this House, but to have the chance of getting on to the treasury benches.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George also complained because he found mentioned in the Speech from the Throne many measures which he said had not been discussed during the last election. I have to remind the hon. gentleman that most of the measures which are forecast in the Speech from the Throne were referred to, all over the country in practically all the speeches delivered by the Prime Minister at the meetings he attended, and such as were not were old measures which had frequently been before the House of Commons in past years. Take, for example, the question of the return of the natural resources. This question has been agitated in parliament for several years and has been the subject of discussion between representatives of the provinces and of the Dominion.
If the matter has not 'been brought to a conclusion as yet, it is because the negotiations were not completed until this year, and until now we were not in a position to promise the measure which had been requested a few years ago. This programme and these discussions are not new. The question has been often debated during previous sessions. The completion of the Hudson Bay railway is not a new thing either. We have been spending money every year upon this work, in maintaining the road in good order and good condition. We have never definitely refused to complete the undertaking. It was a subject of much discussion during the last election, and the Prime Minister is not the only man who might be accused of having made a promise to the people of the west. The right hon. leader of the opposition practically made the same promise although, in his case, there was a proviso that the cost should not be more than $3,000,000. Nevertheless, in principle, it is the same promise.

speechtext:
The question of the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, as I said, was discussed throughout the last campaign and both political parties, Liberals a3 well as Conservatives, are committed to it, so that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has no reason at all to attack the Liberal party because of their promise to bring about the realization of this project, which is so dear to the hearts of the Progressive members. In regard to the other subjects spoken of, the situation is absolutely the same. They are old questions which have been agitated for many years, and now the time has come for the realization of certain of the hopes of my hon. friends from the west. The hon. member in criticising the promises we have made, and our intention to carry out certain demands of the Progressive members, has no serious reason to complain, because the party whose advent to power he is now trying to assist would be forced in the
Government's Right to Office

event, of their succeeding, to make the same concessions that we are now offering the western people. My hon. friend should not find fault with that, although he comes from the great city of Montreal and has been helped by certain newspapers and certain people there who are opposed to any concessions at all to *the west. My hon. friend has no reason at all to oppose any proposals which might help to unite all sections of Canada and bring about a better understanding amongst the citizens as a whole. It is useless to try to develop our country by merely helping a few manufacturers in the city of Montreal; it is futile to try to develop this great country simply by aiding one or two of the various provinces of Canada. If we want to build up this country, if we want to develop our wonderful natural resources, if we want this Dominion to become a great country, we must help all sections of Canada and not limit ourselves to helping one or two provinces.
The sentiments which have been expressed bv my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) are not new to my ears. I have been accused in many newspapers of having aroused .prejudices in this country. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made an incidental reference of that kind the other day. I want to [DOT]tell him that when the opportunity comes I shall answer him as to that, because I can confidently compare my political record with his own. If he looks into the fyles of the various newspapers, he will find no ground for any such action as he attributed to me in the reports of the speeches which I have made in the province of Quebec. He will find however *that the editorials of certain English papers of the city of Montreal were calculated to .mislead the people during the last general election. Liberal members, including myself, were accused of making statements during the last campaign which we never uttered. Throughout the campaign we heard our opponents broadcasting all over the province that the Liberal party should be condemned because it had been making sacrifices for the benefit of the people of the western provinces. We W'ere accused of ruining the industries of Quebec and Ontario, because we had made certain concessions on the tariff to please the western people. Such were the sentiments expressed by our opponents in Quebec in the late campaign; they were against all co-operation between Ontario and Quebec and the western provinces. They wanted the two old provinces to enjoy all the advantages of being in power, but they denied1 any advantage therefrom to the prairie provinces to which

every true Canadian should look for the welfare of Canada as a whole.
I have no further comment to offer upon the speech delivered by the very respectable gentleman representing St. Lawrence-St. George, except to say this: personally, I am ready and the province of Quebec is ready, I may say, to make the sacrifices that are necessary to help the western provinces in trying to bring about a better understanding between the citizens of Canada as a whole. It has been said that the Liberal party made certain sacrifices in order to come to an understanding with the citizens of the west. Yes, we have made sacrifices and we are ready in Quebec, as I think some people are ready in Ontario, to make further sacrifices in order to promote a better understanding between all the Canadian provinces. Surely he should not abject because we are trying to bring about such a desirable result, because we are willing to grant certain requests made by the people of the west.
We are placed at the present time in a very delicate position. It is not a new one, and it is quite a natural one. It is the result of new developments in our political life for which, apparently, rules were not provided in the building of what is now our constitution. We have reached a point where we have possibly to establish our own precedents to deal with the situations in which we might find ourselves. We have here different groups, representing different shades of opinion in our country. Is that a good thing? Is that in reality embarrassing? I need not answer these questions to-night. Are these groups to last long, or are they to be of short duration? Nobody can tell that at this time. Let the House try to see its way through the difficulties and deal, not with precedents, not with nice distinctions, but with facts as they are and as they present themselves to us. Precedents have been cited by very learned gentlemen in this House and distinctions have been made. Interpretations have been offered. All this has reminded me of my legal practice, when I had to fight against precedents or when I had to invoke precedents myself. I have always found, and I think we have all discovered in this House in the last few days, that it is easy to obtain precedents on both sides of an issue. I have a certain respect for precedents, but not for them as such. I have respect for precedents on account of the principle that is sanctioned, not on account of the particular judgment which is expressed by the decision. After all what is a precedent? A precedent is the result of distinction on points of law or of interpret-

ation on. points of law, and very often precedents are based upon facts the accuracy of which is very much disputed. In practice they are met in the same way that they have been met here. They are met first of all with the argument that such precedent is no good; that it should not be applied because it is too old. This was the argument which was advanced by the hon. member for South Wellington in regard to the precedent cited by the Solicitor General. It is said also that such precedent is not applicable to the present circumstances. This argument has been invoked against the precedents cited by the Solicitor General, and if I understood him aright, the hon. member for South Wellington said, "This precedent was established in very exceptional cases and in very difficult and trying circumstances, and we should not apply in the present case a precedent which was invoked under such circumstances." We have heard also, and we hear every day before the tribunals of our country, that such a precedent should not be applied because it is too recent and has not had the advantage of the test of experience. Other precedents are not followed because they are too old. It is rather easy to find1 precedents on all sides of an issue, and practically all precedents are disputable. But above all precedents and judgments there is the supreme thought, the golden principle which has come with an increased brightness through centuries, and, as everybody admits, should govern all our parliamentary institutions, and that principle is that majorities should rule.

speechtext:
If the popular vote were
going to be considered as the opinion of the people which should govern in this country and establish the majority, certain members having been elected by larger majorities would have a right, as a consequence, to speak louder and longer in the House of Commons. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), on account of the huge majority which he received, would have more authority than three or four members of the House of Cotnimons, and certainly he would have more than members sitting behind him who were returned to this House by a minority vote. So, it is very easy to see that we cannot rely upon the popular vote as such. Many reasons may have influenced the result of this election in favour of one particular candidate as against another. The hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) is not here on account of the record of the Tory or Union administration. He is not here on account of the record of the Conservative party. He is here on account of his personality and the goodwill which he enjoys in the constituency of Argenteuil. This is another example to illustrate why we cannot rely upon the popular vote as such. According to our constitution, we have to accept the will of the people when it is expressed ,by their duly elected representatives in this House of Commons. All the members are equal here. Those who have been elected by a small majority have all the rights which those elected by a larger majority may claim for themselves. Under our constitution, our system as it exists at the present
10 p.m. time, ail representatives elected, whatever may have been the vote given them, providing they have a majority, are entitled to sit in this House. If we were going to take the popular vote as already explained, we might have to tell certain hon. gentlemen sitting here, that they had nothing to say, but must wait for the expression of opinion of their electors as indicated by the popular vote cast in their respective constituencies. More particularly in a house constituted as the present House of Commons is, with two, three, four, five, and possibly six groups of men dividing public opinion in Canada, the true will of the people, or, if I may use this expression, the will, constitutionally expressed, of the people, is to be found in the House of Commons when their duly elected representatives are assembled here. Otherwise, there would be chaos; our parliamentary institutions would be of no value

and could not exist, if we were to take into consideration only the popular vote as it is counted after the close of the polls.
It might be said that a prime minister is often called upon to form a government, after the closing of the polls, without any summoning of parliament. But when His Excellency calls upon the leader of a party to form a government, he is not certain, he only assumes that this leader will be in a position to carry with him in the House of Commons a majority of the representatives of the people. He is not relying solely upon the result of the popular vote as cast. He assumes from the popular vote cast at the polls that the leader who has the majority of members elected to support him will be in a position, when in the House, to maintain this majority in favour of the measures that he is going to propose. The challenge is always -made and can be made only as to the majority in the House of Commons. It cannot be made outside of the House of Commons. It does not matter if one group is larger than another, if one is smaller than another. The larger group may be in a minority, if all the minority groups unite. That is the situation at the present time. So, in my humble judgment, the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite form the larger group is of no importance under the present circumstances because, although they have the larger group, they are still in a minority in the House of Commons. The majority, not the group is the essential thing. After the last election, it was found that all the groups were in a minority. My right hon. -friend said: Well, the government, and ithe government, alone was before the people and it is the government which was rejected. We may very well answer -him ,by saying: That might be true, but you have not been elected to deal with the affairs of Canada. You yourself have not been given the majority to command the destinies of our country. What, then, was the course to be followed? The summoning of parliament, the calling together of the representatives of the people to decide the various issues. The resignation of the Prime Minister would not have -made the situation any dearer. The same thing would have happened. Suppose we had resigned and the leader of the opposition had been called upon to form a government, and, having done so, had- convened parliament. He would have been subject to the same attack that has been made upon us in the present situation, and to obtain -a majority and retain power he would have been forced to seek the support of another group in the House. Obviously therefore the position would have been absolutely as it is at the present time. Two courses were

Governm'ent's Right to Office
open to the government, as I have indicated: the government could either meet parliament or iit could advise His Excellency to call upon the leader of the opposition to form an administration. But in giving this advice to His Excellency, it was necessary that the Prime Minister should himself be convinced that the right hon. gentleman was in a position to command a majority in the House of Commons. If the Prime Minister entertained any serious doubt about my right hon. friend's ability to secure a majority in the House, then it was undoubtedly his duty to refrain from advising His Excellency to call upon the right hon. gentleman, for had he done so, he would simply have been inviting chaos.

speechtext:
I am not quoting any statement; I am merely expressing my own humble view of the matter. Was the Prime Minister, then, in a position to convince himself that the leader of the opposition would be able to command a majority in the House, which majority he could secure only by the support of the Progressive party? We may answer this question by considering briefly the circumstances attending the election.
Throughout the campaign the right hon. gentleman's friends and) himself have been attacking the government, because of the fact that it had been on friendly terms with the Progressives during the preceding three years. The government was severely condemned because it had made certain concessions to the Progressive party, small as those concessions were. We were accused of sacrificing the^ interests both of Quebec and of the province of Ontario in order to obtain the support of that party, and we were charged further with responsibility for the closing of our factories as a result of our reduction of the tariff, made, the allegation was, as a means of pleasing Progressive members. And Mr. Patenaude, during the last campaign, in a speech that he cannot deny, because it has been published broadcast throughout the province of Quebec, made the statement that the Liberal party and the Liberal government had practically sold that province and the province of Ontario to the people of the west. These facts were all published and were in the mind of the Prime Minister. Well, does any one contend for a moment that the Prime Minister could reasonably conclude, under the cir-j cumstances, that the leader of the opposition, in view of the stand he had been taking, could secure the support of the Progressive party?
Where is there a man with ordinary common sense, a man capable of thinking for a moment, who believes that the leader of the opposition could hope at that time to obtain the support of the Progressive party? That support may be given him; we do not know. Certainly the invitation that has come from the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is interesting and attractive. But there was something more that operated to convince the Prime Minister of my right hon. friend's inability to command a majority in the House. The Progressives are low tariff men: how therefore can any one think they would approve the policy of the leader of the opposition, who had declared that, if given an opportunity he would increase the tariff on agricultural implements? This declaration of his cannot be denied, for it appears in speeches he has made; he is so reported in Hansard of June 2 last year. A question was put to the right hon. gentleman by the then member for Brantford, Mr. Raymond:	"If you are
returned to power, do you intend to raise the tariff on agricultural implements to the level at which it was when you left office?" And the right hon. gentleman answered, "Undoubtedly, I would, and I give this answer unhesitatingly." There is no doubt whatever that he made this declaration; it cannot be denied. It is therefore a part of his policy to increase the duty on agricultural implements, and such was the interpretation given to his motion presented last session in favour of the revision of the tariff. In view of this fact, does any one with ordinary common sense imagine for a single moment that the right hon. gentleman could reasonably expect the support of the Progressives, with a policy of further increasing the tariff on these implements? No. Under the circumstances the Prime Minister certainly could not recommend to His Excellency that he call upon the right hon. gentleman to form a government, for the facts all indicated beyond the shadow of a doubt that the right hon. gentleman was in no position to command a majority in the House. If therefore the Prime Minister was in doubt in this respect, he had only one course open to him, and that course he followed, namely, to summon parliament in order to have the will of the people expressed through their elected representatives. This was the only logical, the only democratic, the only legal course which the Prime Minister could have followed, although no doubt by a very slight distinction it may be contended that it is not constitutional. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied with the legality of the procedure, and if the course we have followed is legally sound, I do not
Government's Righl to Office

care for the various interpretations, on constitutional grounds, which have been placed upon the position we have taken. Certainly that position cannot be legal and at the same time unconstitutional; nor can it be constitutional and at the same time illegal. That there must be at least some relation between the two, is evident to the common sense of hon. gentlemen representing the people of this country.
I say therefore that the course which the government followed was the only democratic one that could have been followed. It has been said that our position was one of people acting in an autocratic manner. I hold however [DOT] that if we had done what it 'is suggested we should have done, we would then have been acting autocratically, because such a course would have deprived the representatives of the people, composing the groups which we find in this House, of the right to have their say in the matter.
Our position, I repeat, is legal and it is constitutional. Many authorities have been cited on both sides of the House by learned gentlemen who have read considerably from numerous books. Reference has been made to Mr. Gladstone. Well, I have under my hand an extract from Morley's Life of Gladstone in which it is related that in 1874, although Mr. Gladstone did not meet the House, it was his personal opinion that he had a right to do so. Surely that opinion, coming as it does from so eminent an authority, carries weight. Although Mr. Gladstone did not put into practice the view he held, it was undoubtedly his opinion that, had he met parliament, be would have been acting constitutionally; he admitted that he had the right to face the House, just as we are facing it to-day. And being in the House legally-and I add, constitutionally, because our authorities are as good as those cited by our friends opposite 

we are met here by an amendment which has been the subject of very learned discussion on the part of members who have the right to call themselves constitutional lawyers. What is contended in this amendment? It is contended purely and simply that the procedure which we have followed is not the right one; that we are not competent to face the House, and that we have no right to bring down a Speech from the Throne. That is the amendment proposed by the right hon. gentleman, and nothing else. What we have to decide here in the light of the discussion which has taken place is this: Was the government competent; hadi the government authority to meet the House and ask for a decision by the representatives of the 
people? That is the only question. It is not a question of passing judgment upon the past record of 'the Liberal party; it is not a blanket authority given to the administration for the future. The only issue at stake at the present time is to decide if we are competent to face the House and have the question decided by its members. I am in good company when I say that we were right in doing what we did, because the strongest lawyers in favour of the amendment admitted that we were right. The hon. and learned member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has admitted1 very plainly that the government had the right to do what it did-and Jet me remind you that this gentleman was the former Minister of Justice in 'the administration of my right ho-n. friend. He was the first one to attack the contention of his leader in the House. He brought here a mass of documents and authorities, and after studying them he came to the conclusion that we had the right to summon parliament. And he is not alone. Another hon. gentleman whom I esteem very highly, because to my mind he is one of the best debaters in the House of Commons, the hon. member for South Wellington, admitted the same thing -that the government was right in summoning parliament. Answering the argument of the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said: "How can

Everybody knows that a minister after he has been defeated can continue in office for a reasonable time; he continues in office as a minister so long as he does not send in his resignation. So there is nothing extraordinary in a minister being absent from the House, because under our constitution and practice a minister can retain office for a reasonable time after he has been defeated. When the Prime Minister is absent from the House the business of the country is carried on just the same by the other ministers, who are equally advisers of the crown. The affairs of the country are dealt with in just the same wa3', and so it does not matter if the Prime Minister has not a seat in the House of Commons provided that his absence is only temporary. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will not be out of the House of Commons for a longer period of time than would the right hon. leader of the opposition if he should be called as Prime Minister after the vote in this House. If the amendment of my right hon. friend does carry the Prime Minister of to-day will probably advise His Excellency to call on the right hon. leader of the opposition, and he will be sworn in as Prime Minister. The moment he is sworn in, he is out of this House, and it is the same with all his ministers. The House would have to be adjourned and all its business postponed, and we would have to wait three weeks, possibly four, for the election of fifteen or seventeen ministers.
