subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENTS RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are aware it has not been my practice to occupy the time of the House in making long speeches. On the contrary I have always been willing to expedite as much as possible the transaction of the business of parliament. On this occasion, however, I would like to offer a few remarks on the subject engaging the attention of the House.
I have listened very carefully to the indictment by my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) and his able and eloquent lieutenants of the gentlemen now professing to constitute the government of this country. 'I have listened just as attentively to -the defence offered by those gentlemen of their status, and it seems to me the position we now find ourselves in is that since the 2:9th of October last Canada has had a government without a head, ana that since this House met on the seventli instant we have had neither a governmental head nor a government. Strange as it may appear, the modern precedent that our friends opposite most strongly urge in support of the conduct of this alleged government in clinging to office is the action of the right hon, leader of the opposition in 1921 when, failing of election in his own constituency and ceasing to be the leader of the largest group, he with very little delay took the necessary steps and secured election to parliament from another constituency willing to elect him. The course pursued by the right hon. gentleman at that time was vehemently denounced by the then leader of the opposition, now the ex-Prirne Minister, Mr. King. It was denounced at that time by him as entirely unconstitutional, yet that very precedent is now urged in justification for the present conduct of the exPrime Minister. In the following (language ex-Prime Minister King expressed his decided disapproval of the course of my right hon. leader:
I can only say at the moment that such a violation of constitutional procedure can scarcely fail to bring the severest censure upon Mr. Meighen, a censure which the party he leads must also share if it countenances such an act.
14011-12 #

Just whether this high-handed and unwarranted course on Mr. Meiglien's part can be defended on technical or legal grounds remains to be seen. That it is morally indefensible I do not hesitate to say. , One thing is certain; the Canadian public will not fail to recognize, nor Canadian political history to record, that Mr. Meighen's last act as Prime Minister, like his first, was one of usurpation.
Not sure that it was unconstitutional, but quite sure that it was morally wrong. That is how Mr. King described the precedent that is advanced now by his followers here as justification for the course which he has pursued, evidently with the idea that in their eyes two wrongs, if one was a wrong, make a right.
In reality, IMr. Speaker, there is a vast difference between the two teases. Let us briefly examine them. In 1921, on failure of election in the district of Portage la Prairie the right hon. leader of the Conservative partjr as soon as possible became a candidate in the district of Grenville. He was elected, and so became entitled to all the rights of a member of parliament. He qualified himself to function as such, and proceeded to function to the great advantage of his country and of his party, and evidently to the great discomfiture of hon. gentlemen opposite. On the other hand what was the course of ex-Prime Minister King, ex-member of parliament? He does not deem it worth while to qualify as a member of parliament either by seeking election to this House or by appointment to the Senate. Yet he assumes to be Prime Minister, to hang on to the office of Prime Minister; and I presume he will	claim-probably is
claiming and receiving-tfhe emoluments of the office without being a member of parliament.	*
Mr. King is reported in the press of the country as taking the high moral ground that the Liberal group should not make appointments, should not function as a government, and in this respect no one will quarrel with him. But how about his own case? Is he consistent in that regard? Does he live up to the high ideal which he has proclaimed?
It is all very well to refrain from other appointments, but how about the office of Prime Minister? One may be pardoned for referring to that hon. gentleman's own words to describe his conduct. This is what he says:
That it is morally indefensible I do not hesitate to say.
Surely those words are not too strong in referring to Mr. King's present course. He has not been a member of parliament since
October 29 last, yet he professes to assume -and shall I, in his language, say usurp?-
Government's Right to Office

the office of Prime Minister, an office to which only a member of parliament can attain. He actually comes to this House when not a member. He pretends to be Prime Minister and in that assumed role-or, as he would put it, that usurped role-he actually meets His Excellency at the portals of this House and escorts him to the seat of honour. If the positions of the two leaders were reversed, if one could imagine my leader putting himself in that ridiculous position, what adjectives would Mr. King use to describe the situation? Certainly something much stronger than those he used in 1921. It would be interesting to be able to look behind the mask of officialdom and good breeding and to read what was actually taking place in the mind of Byng of Vimy, and to know what he actually thought of his escort on that occasion. It cannot be controverted, Mr. Speaker, that ex-Prime Minister King has not been a member of parliament since 29th October. He cannot enter either house of parliament. He is neither a member of the Commons nor of the Senate. The constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, says that parliament shall consist of the sovereign-that is the Governor General, -the Senate or upper house, and the House of Commons. Now the ex-Prime Minister is no part of parliament, and, of necessity, not being a part of parliament, he cannot be Prime Minister. We have no Prime Minister and no government and there is no use pretending that we have. It has been observed often with pride that we Britishers have no written constitution hedging us in and hampering us between its four walls; that we play the game according to unwritten rules, well defined and well understood. How can we continue to carry on under that system if public men fail to play the game. We will soon require to have a written rule to hold some people.
Speaking in defence and in approval of the manner in which his leader is playing the game, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) -I will not use his leader's expression and say the gentleman who is usurping the position of Minister of Justice-said the other day:
I rise to-day to defend the public honour of the right hon. the leader of the government and to show that not only had he the right to do that, but that it was his supreme duty to do it. Any other attitude on his part would have been a breach of trust, an infringement of the rights of parliament.
The hon. gentleman would have the House and the country believe that Mr. King is doing the only thing it was open to him to do. Anything else, as it was put, would have been a breach of trust and an infringement on the rights of parliament. Surely that is, to use a slang expression, "a bit thick". Does it

not occur to Mr. King and the Minister of Justice that there was one thing he might have done, one obviously manifest thing he should have done, and that was to resign- that is if it is necessary to resign when one fails of election? I have been a defeated candidate. I did not have to resign. The electors attended to that for me, as they have done in Mr. King's case. The difference is that he persists in ignoring their verdict. I did not attempt to function as a member of parliament until elected on a subsequent occasion. Mr. King assumes to foe much more than a member of parliament. He assumes to be Prime Minister without the qualification of an.election. It is a wonder he went to the formality and the trouble of standing as a candidate at all in North York, if he could be Prime Minister without election. Are there two members for North York? Apparently there are, one elected and one defeated. The defeated1 one, notwithstanding that fact, is Prime Minister, and the other is only a private member.
If hon, members of the Progressive group would like to hear a rule of conduct that was laid down by one whose opinion should have great weight with them, and now should have great weight with members of the Liberal party, I would like to quote what was said on 17th April, 1923, on the eve of the last election campaign in Ontario. Mr. Drury, the head of the United Farmers of Ontario government, made the following statement:
In order that, there may be no doubt whatever as to my position I take this opportunity of stating it clearly and unequivocally. If, after the election I find myself in command of a clear majority of the House I will of course continue to carry on the Government. If I find that either of the other parties has a clear majority of the House I will at once in accordance with sound constitutional procedure advise His Honour to call on the leader of that party to form a government.
If, on the other hand I find myself the leader of a party which, while in the minority, is still the largest party in the House I will carry on the government relying on and accepting such support as the merit of my record and policy may bring us.
If there should be elected a group or party larger than that of which I am the head, though not large enough to command a clear majority of the House I will advise His Honour to call on the leader of that party to form the government.
That is what Mr. Drurv said, and that is what I submit any manly man would say. Certainly it is a more manly course than that now pursued by this government. What would happen if other defeated ministers declined to accept the verdict of the electors and clung to office and emolument? What about democracy and the rights of the people, so dear to Mr. King? Other ministers and other members of parliament have exactlv

Government's Right to Office
the same right to cling as Mr. King has. and what a lovely state of affairs we would have if they undertook to do so. And if he does so. why not they?
Now what has led up to the present situation in this House? A comparison of the Speech from the Throne of this year with the Speeches of the years 1922, 1923, 1924 and 1926 shows repeated references to many subjects upon which legislation and fulfilment of promises never materialized-old grandstand plays repeated. But in the Speech from the Throne of 1926 we find that reforms and important questions to which reference was made and which the government promised to deal with in 1925 and failed have been omitted altogether. I will just quote two. I quote first from the Speech from the Throne in 1925-and to those of us who were here during that session of 1925 it will recall most interesting incidents. The Speech from the Throne says:
With regard to ocean freight rates, action is being taken to overcome the restraints on export trade due to the exactions of the powerful steamship combine known as the North Atlantic Steamship Conference. Your approval will be asked of a measure aimed at affording the government of Canada a control of ocean rates.
We remember the introduction of that Petersen contract by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce. We remember when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), following the minister, pointed out the undesirable features of that contract and ventured to suggest that the government, in wishing to refer it to a select committee, would be only too glad to have important changes made in it, to have it trimmed up. We remember how the then Prime Minister arose in his place and announced that the government would stand for no change in the contract; that not a line, not a word would be changed; that they would stand or fa'll by it, and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre expressed his satisfaction and said that that was the first time he had ever heard the Prime Minister say that he would stand by anything. Those of us who were here then remember, as if it were yesterday, when the next member of this House rose tc speak, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), who has spoken here to-night, and attacked the contract quite as severely, if not more so, than-the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, how quickly the then Prime Minister changed his attitude. He rose and assured the hon. member for Red Deer and the Progressive group that they had misunderstood him. Stand or fall by the contract! Why, 14011-12J
they could do anything they liked with that contract and he would be glad to accept it if they would only continue him in office. The (same plea is being made by the remnant of the government to-day. Office is all that concerns them. On that memorable day the Prime Minister climbed down quickly. Jn that same Speech from the Throne, I find these words:
You will be asked to sanction the calling of a conference between the federal and provincial governments to consider the advisability of amending the British North America Act with respect to the constitution and powers of the Senate.	.
That is a very mild statement when considered in the light of the bold statement made by the Prime Minister in the closing hours of the preceding session. Then he (promised the House and the country that he would bring in a measure to reform the Senate. When less than twelve months had gone by, we find this anaemic paragraph in the Speech from the Throne promising a conference of the provinces. Was anything done with that? Was it followed up in the House? Was the conference ever held? Has that reform been accomplished? How has this government concluded to reform the Senate? By allowing Providence to remove the Conservative members and by Mr. Mackenzie King appointing (Liberals and putting his ministers in that haven of rest in the Senate, fleeing from the wrath of the people. A wonderful reform of the Senate! Surely our Liberal friends give members of this House, including members of the Progressive group, credit for some ability to judge of their insincerity and credit for some memory. Surely 11 p.m. they cannot think we have forgotten their broken pledges of economy. The word "economy" runs through all their Speeches from the Throne. In each the government promises strict economy. Surely they cannot think we have forgotten their broken promises of free and freer trade, of sound immigration policies, of rural credits, of proportional representation, of the alternative vote, of the extermination of combines and trusts, of the control of the Great Lakes freights, their fake surpluses, the promised Senate reform, their expensive royal commissions and many other matters on which the House was allowed to waste much time, but on which the House, lacking a lead from the government, divided itself so that these proposals came to naught. To members in doubt whether they should now vote for the amendment before the House, the fact that the defeat of this amendment will mean a continua-

Government's Right, to Office
lion of the weak, vacillating, aimless government which Canada has had for the past four years, should be sufficient to help them in .making up their minds.
It is gratifying to me, as it must be to my right hon. leader and to those supporting him ;to hear, during the course of this debate, member after member of the Progressive party rise in his place and say publicly that he had every confidence in the integrity and sincerity of the leader of the Conservative party and express the belief that he and they would staijd by their .pledges and carry out their .announced policies, while they had no such faith in the ex-Prime Minister or the Liberal group of members opposite. That being so, *how can members of the Progressive .party bring themselves to support the remnant of this Liberal government in anything which it .may bring before the House?
We have had quoted in this debate the opinion of one very prominent citizen of Canada, indeed, that of the most prominent Canadian, of Mr. Mackenzie King himself, the former Prime Minister, on the government of the [past four years. In effect, he says that the government was a failure, an impossibility. That is the reason he had an election. Some of his words have been already quoted; but they are so conclusive and So much more applicable to the present situation than that of which he spoke that they are worth repeating :
As I have already said, I have not the least doubt we shall be able to command such support as we all along have had in the House of Commons at another session; but shall we be able to do more than that ? That is the question I have put to every one of my colleagues in the government, and to not a few of the members. It is a question I now put to you who have honoured me with your representation in the House of Commons. It is a question I put to the electorate of this country. Is it sufficient that as a government we should continue in office, drawing our indemnities and salaries as members and ministers, and enjoying the other fruits of office, when great national questions press for solution, with which for want of an adequate majority in Parliament we are unable satisfactorily to cope? ... I would say further, I do not believe that any one of the four-
Speaking of the four great questions the government found it necessary to deal with.
-can be dealt with effectively by a government which is not supported by a substantial majority in the House of Commons. Group government and minority government may be inevitable in transitional phases of our political history, but neither is the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms.
In those words Mr. King admitted failure on his part, admitted that the government should no longer carry on. That is his opinion of his own government; thait, as a matter of fact, is his real opinion of the situation to-day, and that is the opinion of his ministers. There

is no doubt about that because his government is much weaker to-day than it was then. Will any hon. member dispute that fact? Is the loss of the Prime Minister nothing? He has gone. Is the loss of the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Labour, the trust-busting Minister of Labour-
That is nothing.

Some hon. members say that is nothing; but I do not think the members of the government think it. is nothing. Was the loss of the Minister of Immigration nothing? Did the loss of the Minister of Trade and Commerce not weaken the government? Didi the loss of some four other ministers not weaken the government? If they were weiak before they lost them and the fifteen private members who went down to defeat along with them, what is the condition to-day? If the Prime Minister then felt they could not function to the benefit and satisfaction of the Canadian people, how can they ask the people of Canada to keep them in power in their present dilapidated state? What is the use of it? What good will the country derive from it? What will anyone get out of it except the emoluments of office which the members of the government and their followers will annex? The national problems to which the Prime Minister referred in that election speech of his have not [DOT] yet been solved. Can this aggregation now calling itself a government do any more towards solving them? They admitted before the election that they could not. The fact of the matter is that Mr. King has put himself out of cotirt; he has delivered judgment against himself. Let hon. members who are in doubt as to how they Should vote follow Mr. King's advice. I have read you some of his words; let me quote him further:
I refer now to all important national problems that are pressing for solution, and which cannot be solved in a parliament constituted after the manner of a parliament elected in 1921, or by any government which does not command a substantial majority in the House of Commons.
How, then, are these unsolved problems to be handled by this government? Surely the government now in office will not urge that it has a substantial majority in this House. But apart from this practical aspect of the question, which should be sufficient to decide any wavering member, there is another consideration which we as Canadians cannot afford to lose sight of. What about the British spirit which the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) so vehemently proclaimed as more important, more desirable than British precedent, than British policy,

Government's Right to Office
more important to him than even the British Empire which he announced as something indifferent to himself? The British spirit defined is after all the spirit of good sportsmanship; that is the very essence of the spirit of British institutions. It is instilled into the British people from the cradle; it is the dominating spirit of the British public schools and of the British universities. And that spirit goes out with them into all parts of the world, and gains for them the respect of all nations. They play the game, as they say: they play the game in politics, they play the game in business and they play the game in sport. They observe the rules, unwritten though they be. Certain things are simply not done; there is no need to ask why. They are not good form and they are not done, and that is all there is to it. Now, we Canadians pride ourselves on being good, clean sports. But what has happened in CanadS? Mr. King, the leading Canadian citizen, challenged us to play. He dissolved parliament for a trial of strength and we accepted the challenge and played on his own terms. Mr. King lost the game; he was struck out and yet he tries to remain at the bat. This notwithstanding, the Minister of Customs ,(Mr. Boivin)) this afternoon extolled to the House the Prime Minister's high sense of honour and propriety. Picture the unlovely spectacle of a British cricketer fairly bowled out and yet in violation of the British spirit clinging to the place he has lost. That is the situation in Canadian politics to-day- an unlovely spectacle in the eyes of the world. Can any sport-loving member of the House be a party to such unsportsmanlike conduct? Surely no one with a drop of sporting blood in his veins can approve, much less support, such a course. I say to hon. members, play the game and do not stifle or besmirch the British spirit. The government could meet, and did meet the House; that is demonstrated by the fact that they are here-'those that are left of them at any rate. But they did not do so fairly. They have acted in violation of that British spirit, for the game was fairly played, and they know it. I say therefore that the largest group in the House should be given an oppportunity to form and attempt to carry on the government; and this the Prime Minister in violation of the British spirit has refused.

Since the present debate began we have listened to a number of able and eloquent speeches on both sides of the House by legal authorities who have won not only a national but, I believe, an empire-wide reputation. For myself I am free to admit that I am unable to
discuss the question with either a legal or technical knowledge, and I shall therefore endeavour to consider it entirely from the layman's point of view. Everyone will agree with me that as we meet in parliament to-day we are confronted by a unique siuation such as has never been witnessed before in Canadian parliamentary history. I agree quite heartily with the suggestion which was thrown out the other day by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), and also by the hon. member for 'Lafoelle (Mr. Bourassa), that if it were possible the members elected to represent the people should should come down here holding more or less independent views and form a composite cabinet and try by co-operation to carry on the government in the national interests. Personally I believe this would work out to the satisfaction of the various classes and the various industries we have in this country. I know there are many hon. gentlemen of the two old parties who repudiate this idea and are of the opinion that it is impractical. Let us remember, however, that the two-party system has not always been in practice even in Great Britain. We can go back to the time in British history when the monarchical form of government exercised power, and I have no doubt that when the people of those days attempted to wrest the power from the monarchy all sorts of fears were entertained that revolution would ensue and that the destruction of the state would be inevitable. But when it became evident that the monarchical form of government was no longer able to cope with the changes of time it had to go. The reason we have groups in this country to-day is the fact that the party system of government has failed to meet the will of the people. It has not been elastic enough to take in every phase of our development. Why was it that our farmers' group started in Canada? Was it because the farmers desired to enter political life simply in order to obtain the honour and power that went with it? Absolutely not; it was because they felt that they had not been receiving justice at the hands of either of the old political parties since confederation. According as our people advance in civilization and in education they are going to demand an increasing share in the government of the country. The people are going to do more thinking for themselves, and unless the political parties that we have in Canada to-day are prepared to adapt themselves to the changing situation then the time in my opinion at least, is not far distant when those parties will disappear. Let me quote in words better than I can express:

Government's Right to Office
New times demand new measures and new men;
The world advances and in time outgrows the law
Which in our fathers' time seemed best;
And doubtless after us some better scheme
Will be worked out by wiser men than we,
Made wiser by the steady growth of truth.
I am fair enough to admit that while I believe the group system is coming, I agreed with the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) when he said the other day that he was not in favour of turning any sharp corners. I believe the time is not ripe for that \vet. When one looks at the spirit of this parliament, with the antagonism shown between the two major parties, it is impossible to believe that they could get together in any spirit of co-operation. Therefore 1 believe we have to face the situation as we find it and deal with it in the best way possible.
There has been a great deal of argument as to whether the amendment involves a vote of confidence, or raises a purely constitutional question. I have already stated that 1 have very little confidence in either of the two old parties. During the last four years I have heard each party hurl accusations across the floor at the other, and they have washed a great deal of dirty linen. I want to say to both parties that so far as I can judge there is enough brush in both to bum them to cinders.
To come down to the purely constitutional aspect, from my point of view I feel very strongly on this question, and I believe that we are establishing a precedent at the present time which may prevail for many years to come. 1 want to say I am very sorry to have to disagree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), for whom I have the greatest respect. In the last four years we have been able to see eye to eye on many questions which have been before this House, but while I heartily agree with him when he says that the group system is coming, I cannot agree that in establishing ' the principle that the largest group should first be given the opportunity of forming a government we will in any way interfere with the introduction of the group system into this House. My opinion is that if the Labour group, which at present consists of only two members, should develop in Canada as it has done in Great Britain, and come back after an election with the largest group, it would be^only right and proper that they should first be called on to form a government and present their policies to parliament. That does not necessarily mean that if their policies did not meet with the approval of the other groups, they would be sustained, but they should at least be given the first opportunity.	.

Let us look back to the time when the Baldwin government came into power in Great Britain, just a few years ago. They came back after the election in a minority, but they were the largest group and therefore had a perfect right to come to parliament and present their Speech from the Throne. They were defeated and the minority group headed by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald was then called upon to form a government, which in my opinion was quite proper. Then let us look at the situation in Ontario in 1919, when the Hearst government appealed to the country. They came back as a minority group, which is the situation here to-day, with a larger group opposing them, neither having a majority in the House. What was the result? Mr. Hearst immediately resigned and left it to the lieutenant-governor to call on the head of a larger group to form a government. The result was that the Farmer group, at that time although in a minority, in co-operation with Labour, were able to form a government and carry on for some years.
In establishing this principle I feel that I am taking an absolutely independent stand, and not favouring either the Liberal or the Conservative party. I say that for this reason, that in casting my vote on this occasion it is true it might place the Conservatives in office, but if the situation were reversed and we had the Liberals with the largest group, it would mean that the Liberals would go into office. Therefore I think I am standing by the principle and taking an absolutely independent stand in the matter.
Npw let us look at the results of the last election. That election was not forced on the government. They chose their own time, and the Prime Minister stated then, as the House has already been reminded, that the reason he could not carry out his programme was because he had not a majority. He was appealing to the countiy for that majority, and he said that if he did not get it he would ask for dissolution. In the last election it was a well recognized fact that the Progressive party, even though every candidate was elected, could not form a government because of their lack of numbers. Therefore the contest in the last election, as to who would form a government, was between the two major parties. And what was the result? As between these major parties I do not think it can be disputed by anyone that the Conservatives had the largest popular vote in the country, and also the largest number of members of any group returned to the House. Only at one time have the people an opportunity of expressing their will, and that is at

Government's Right to Office
an election. The people at the last election showed by their vote, both the popular vote and the representatives in this House, that while they did not give a mandate to either party they at least did show a preference, and in my opinion the will of the people should not be flouted. The party shown that preference should first be called upon to form a government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have listened to many able arguments on both sides, some short and some more lengthy. I believe our minds are pretty well made up, and I would not have spoken in this debate had it not been for the fact that there have been honest differences of opinion in this corner of the House, and I felt it my duty after having come to the conscientious decision to which I have come, to at least explain the reason why I will have to support this amendment.

Mx.
Speaker, seeing that so many speeches from learned men of this Dominion have been directed to this part of the House during the last three or four days, I have come to the conclusion that the presence of the Progressive party bears some significance in our public life at this time. Indeed', Sir, it reminds me of a young lady I knew once who had some trouble in deciding 'between two suitors both seeking her favour; but I would pity any young lady who saw so little difference between the two suitors as the Progressive party is seeing between the two parties who to-day are craving our favour.
We are discussing what appears to be a most unique subject for this parliament, indeed, for any parliament. We have had an election to decide the policies of this country. Different parties, so-called, have appealed to the people for their confidence. I think it may be well for a minute to define what is meant by a party, k party, as known in politics, is a group of men that have gathered themselves aroimd a set of principles in an endeavour to bring those principles into effect. The Liberal party is, per se, the people's party, the party that stands for progress along lines of principle favourable to the common people, the workers on the land, and the name as applied indicates a person or group that advocates freedom of thought or of action in political matters. Liberalism is a freedom from bigotry, or narrowness or selfishness.
Conservatism literally means opposition to change. A Conservative is one who is disposed to maintain existing conditions, an advocate of class distinctions and privileges; so says the dictionary.
There are two parties in this House at present, and only two, on principle, the one composed of the Labour representatives, and the Progressive party, to which I belong. They together may well be called the Liberal party. A number who call themselves Liberal but who are by nature advocates of class privilege and class distinctions, on whichever side of the House they may sit, must be classed as Conservatives. This Conservative party has been inaugurated, and has been maintained, by the inauguration of class privilege many years ago. This was a system of legislation freely called by Sir Richard Cartwright since 1878, when he was in parliament, legalized robbery. These beneficiaries of privilege, or legalized robbery, per Sir Richard Cartwright, have dominated this House of Commons, and it does not matter that they divide themselves up into two groups called Conservatives on the one side of the House, and, in error, Liberals on the other; they both belong in one party. Indeed, taking the last four years as a criterion of the legislation enacted in this House since 1897 in particular, the advocates of class privilege and class distinctions have dominated entirely this House of Commons. It is this infidelity on their part to their nominal platform or professions of principle that has brought the country to the present impasse in which we now find ourselves. The beneficiaries of privilege over the whole of this Dominion to-day dominate the Conservative party and the so-called Liberal party, and there is no doubt in my mind that to-day we are making ourselves a laughing stock in political circles the world over. Both parties are appealing to-day to the people's party, the Progressive party, to put them in power, and we of the Progressive party have to decide, what is there in principle that would warrant a decision one way or the other. Both parties stand for class privilege and class distinctions. Both want to get the reins of government, as that is a great advantage in the next election, which in all probability will soon be called, and the country will again be plunged into the turmoil and expense of another political contest because the parties who in practice, in this House claim the right to rule are not divided on principle. It is a sad thing, Sir, for any nation when it loses itself in a maze of selfishness. The political leaders of this Dominion have led us into and are to-day responsible for the ridiculous position we are now in. Privilege is enthroned, and1 legalized robbery is maintained by misrepresentation of facts on the hustings, the intimidation of workers in our industrial centres, control of the press, and the corruption of

Government's Right to Office
electors throughout the country at election time by federal and provincial party means.
I want to say, Sir, that the two party system of government has come to an end in Canada. It has come to an end for one or two very good reasons:	First, because there has been
allowed a control from outside that has at last obliterated entirely lines of principle. Surely there can be some way found whereby the government of the country can be continued on other than the two party system. It was this lack of principle in that system that brought the third and perhaps the fourth party into this House. It was agreed, when the last election was called, that the real purpose of that election was to eliminate from politics in this country, the third party or Progressive party. I want to say that the Progressive party is going to live. It is going to live because what it advocates is right. We seek no privilege, we seek no class advantage, we only seek legislation that will benefit the entire country. What we are seeking is freedom, and freedom people will have. The Conservative party, promises nothing but bondage, and increase of bondage, high freight rates without the prospect of a nearer outlet to the sea through the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. Indeed taken altogether, their policy as presented in this House since I have been a member is entirely one favouring privilege. Under the circumstances can we decide in favour of that party?
The Liberal party offer the Hudson Bay railway. It is to be completed forthwith. If I do not mistake the meaning of the word "forthwith" it means immediately, without delay whatever the circumstances and whatever the cost. In this impression I ani bome out by the speech of the member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) yesterday and to-day. A measure of relief is also promised from high rates of interest on agricultural credits. These are the things that are promised and they commend themselves to our people. Of course there is the experience of the last four years to be remembered. Where then do we stand?
The amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition is for the most part a legal quibble trying to decide if it is constitutional for the Liberal party, who came back from the election with a smaller number of supporters than the Conservative party, to hold office. In some way I believe it also embodies a vote of non-confidence. Now, many precedents have been given in the argument pro and con, and I should like to bring one more to the attention of the right hon. leader of the opposition. If he had 
followed the example of Mr. Clynes, for instance, when he brought in his vote of confidence on January 17, 1924, there would have been no mistaking the meaning of the present amendment. The amendment moved by Mr. Clynes on that occasion was in these w'ords:
But it is our duty respectfully to submit to Your Majesty that Your Majesty's present advisers have not the confidence of this House.
I think these few words better express the real meaning than the present amendment does and in about one-tenth of the language. I am not a lawyer, and I know very little of constitutional practice, but if a decision has to foe made as to the right to hold office I think parliament is the proper authority to decide, particularly in view of the fact that neither of the parties has been returned with a majority. We are moving forward. As I say the days of the two party system are drawing to an end. Old things are passing away and new ones are taking their place. There is a definite democratic principle involved in this decision. I think parliament is the right authority to decide the majority that shall carry on the government. It is only majorities that can really be recognized, and parliament must decide as to the majority in this instance. Whichever way I vote on this amendment I want the House and those who sent me here to understand that I am not giving unreservedly my support to the legislation that may be brought down later by either party. I must say there was no need for citing so many precedents in this matter. We do not need to go over the whole of history for examples as to the course we should pursue. Even after listening with great interest to the speech of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) yesterday I notice that in all the historic incidents he related he did not give one precedent where a government, returning after an election with the second largest group handed over the reins of office to another group who were also in a minority.

Is the hon. gentleman
not aware of the case in the province of Ontario where the Hearst government handed over the reins of office to the Drury government?

I was not aware that the
hon. member for Fort William quoted that as a precedent.

I did not quote any precedents at all. I simply argued from the standpoint of the majority of the people in the country voting against this government. I was arguing that the people, irrespective of

Government's Right to Office
the Progressives, voted against this government by over 200,000.

I cannot see yet that it
alters the fact that the Tory party have come back as a minority group.
Just a word further as it regards our position. I was rather amused to hear the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) say in his speech the other day that the Progressive party was brought into being by the sins of the Union government. Permit me to say that this organization came into being as a result of the doings of monopolies that controlled the marketing of our products as far back as twenty-five years ago. It is true that we did not organize for political adtion until nineteen years afterwards. It is also true that was during the administration of the Union government, but it was not because anything new in the way of political abuses had transpired. The fact was we had come to a time when we thought we could better redress our grievances by taking a hand in legislation. The time is past in Canada for the old two party system or the two old parties to reign supreme in this House. The people are no longer content to listen to the staged sham fights of days gone by. We have been accused of being a class group, selfishly seeking benefits for ourselves. I want to say that for many years, particularly since 1897, both the Liberal and Conservative parties in this country have constituted a class group who have selfishly ridden on the backs of the primary producers, particularly the argiculturists. Now we have this group in the House representing a class that was hitherto not represented in parliament, that is, the agriculturists. So far as our organization is concerned, the people organize themselves and finance their own election. Their candidates did not have to be endorsed by the heads of any parties. We are the people's party. We are not afraid to publish the sources of our campaign fund. Indeed, sir, judging by the methods employed by some of the candidates of the Liberal and Conservative parties throughout this country, we are no more careful about our 14,000 indemnity than they are. We do not have to purchase any votes to be elected. I was greatly struck the other day by an article in Sir John Willison's magazine, an article which anyone not familiar with the old time methods of election should read if he wants to learn something of the corrupting, debasing, disgraceful and shameful methods of this centralized control. Sir John Willison says:
In too many cases wealthy candidates are grossly plundered. Too often the grants from the centra! fund never get out of the hands of the party middlemen. Contributions, too, are made with the expectation of a twofold return from governments. There is corruption in the constituencies and direct purchase of administrative or legislative favours.
I hope this country is getting away from such methods. The Progressive party to-day has shown the country how to organize and to get away from them, as Sir John Willison explained that it might. I do not think anyone will accuse Sir John Willison of not knowing what he is talking about. In this article he pleads for a system such as ours. For my part I am glad to realize that the country is moving on, and parliament will have to adapt itself to the new system. It is possible that for a long time to come or never there may be no party in this House with a decisive majority-perhaps never. Constitution may be based on precedent, but I want to say in conclusion that I am not going to help to create a precedent that will make it constitutional in the future to give the government over to the largest party while that party is in the minority. I think parliament should see to that.
If as a result of the election on October 29 the Progressive party had been returned to the House with the largest group, would you or would you not expect the Progressive party to form a government?
No, I should say plainly not, unless we were in the majority; unless we represented over fifty per cent of the people of this country.

There are one or two distinctions which I would like, if I can in my humble layman's way, make a little clearer. The constitutional lawyers on both sides have had a good deal of fun poked at them, and I think with some justification- and by the way they have also taken up a good deal of the time of the House in fine hair-splitting. I propose now to indulge in a little fine hair-splitting myself from a layman's point of view. The situation as I see it, is roughly this: the 'Conservatives say that the government in the elections in October had their majority reduced, that the Conservatives increased their following in this House, and that therefore the government should have resigned. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) says so at page 55 of Hansard. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) says so at page 14 of Hansard, and the hon. member for 'South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) says so at page 92-and by the way, that hon. member made the statement most emphatically, of all. There is no dispute about it in his mind: the government should have resigned directly the election was over. The amendment does not say this. The amend-
Government's Right to Office

ment is very careful not to say it. I will put a proposition to the House and ask if it is not a fair one: if the elections had resulted in an overwhelming mandate to a group, other than the party in office, unquestionably the minority group should have resigned. I do not think there would have been any question about that; whether or not they had a Prime Minister in the House would make no difference. But if there was any reasonable doubt, mark you, as to the majority so far as public opinion was concerned on major national policies, then I am satisfied the administration was right in calling a meeting of parliament, presenting itself to the House with a policy, and asking for the support of the House upon it. I do not think 1 need dwell any longer on that point.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie admits the legality of the position of the administration. He does not question it at all. At page 97 of Hansard he states:
I stated that they could legally justify themselves, but that it was not the best constitutional practice.
It might be constitutional practice, but was not the best constitutional practice. The statement of the hon. member for South Wellington at page 92 on this particular point is probably worth reading to the House. He admits not only the legality of the position but also the probability of the constitutionality of the administration's position if one certain thing had happened, namely, the election of the Prime Minister to a seat in the House. At page 92 of Hansard the hon. member says:
I say again that when he knew the result of the vote, when he saw that the popular vote was against him, his duty according to the constitution, was to retire.
I grant that if there is ground for a reasonable doubt there is something to be said in favour of his meeting the House, provided he has a seat.
There was no major objection, therefore, either on legal or on constitutional grounds, to the administration carrying on until parliament met. The only major objection raised in the amendment is that the government cannot function now because of the absence of the Prime Minister. Well, here, we come to the very ticklish point-and this is where the lawyers have done most of their hair splitting. Who can assert that the Prime Minister does not intend to take a seat in the House? Yet the whole argument of the hon. gentlemen to your left, Mr. Speaker, is based upon the assumption that he will not-indeed, that he cannot. It is a most absurd position to take. They argue that because there is no Prime Minister in the House the administration cannot function. I do not know, but I am inclined to think they are confusing the functions of an executive

body, which are extra-parliamentary, with the functions of a committee of parliament, which are	intra-parliamentary.
As I look at the situation, this question occur? to me: Suppose the Liberal party had been returned to this House with an overwhelming majority, 200 members on that side and 45 od this side, but no Prime Minister, would there be no government? Could we not function? Would all these charges be levelled at the present administration? Would there be a demand that they resign office? Can hon. members not see the absurd position into which their hair-splitting brings them? Yet we have to listen to this howl about chaotic conditions and all the rest of it. What more chaotic condition can they imagine than the resignation of the administration at the close of the election, the forming of a government by a minority group which was defeated in the election just as the Liberal party was- for they have no majority in the House-and their meeting a House unquestionably opposed to them on major policies? The history of the last four years definitely sets the Progressive group against the Conservative group. The declared line of policy of the Conservatives, their own statements in this House, have alienated any possible support from any portion of the group to which I belong. Had they offered reasonable co-pperation; had they said to us: We are willing to get together and endeavour to form a Ico-operative administration looking to honourable, frank, stable business government, we might have had some ground for putting this administration out and our Conservative friends in.	What is the
position? The hon. member for West Calgary, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, even the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) intimated .most dearly that there was to be no truck with the Progressives; that they had no bids to make-and they slammed -the door in our faces. Is that a favourable position for them to take as a minority group? How can they now say: If we are put into office, we will carry on for one year or two years; it is all right, your indemnities are safe-and all the rest of it. Their position is absurd.
We find, therefore, that everything is orderly, legal and constitutional down to the time that the administration met parliament. Does any hon. member to the left of Mr. Speaker claim that the administration had no right to advise the crown before parliament met? No. No one has done that. No one dare do it. They were the properly, legally constituted advisers of th,e crown. As such they drafted the Speech from the Throne, a speech which

Government's Right to Office
I may say frankly, has gone out to the whole western Country and has been received with approval. Of course we have had Speeches from the Throne on previous occasions that promised many things, and gave but little- that never bore fruit. But they were presented under entirely different circumstances from those under which the Speech came down in this instance. For me to say that it is useless for us to attempt to co-operate with the government until the promises contained in the Speech from the Throne are implemented, is to deny our own power. I refuse to olace myself in that ridiculous position. I have told my people that I will sup-12 m. port any administration that will give to the country the legislation which, in -my opinion, the country should have. The legislation in the Speech from the Throne, so far as I have been able to analyse it, is good legislation. It is favourable to the part of the country from which I come, and indirectly it will be of benefit tc the whole of Canada. Am I to go back to my people and say: I rejected that; I would not consider it at all, because the leader of the opposition introduced a political amendment, drew a red herring across the trail and through a political trick, attempted to divert me from a plain businesslike course? What have they offered? No truck or trade- the same old thing. The old words ring so familiarly. Nothing to do with the Progressives, you see! They are reciprocity men. No truck or trade with the Yankees over the line, or with the Progressives from western Canada! That is an amazing, a regrettable position, a position which, I venture to say, will have a more far-reaching effect upon the future of the Conservative party than any other position taken by them within the last four years.
Very well, we have got this far. The Speech from the Throne was properly initiated by the advisers of His Majesty. Parliament was called together. By the way, here we come to that via media again, that peculiar line of communication that was missing, that extraordinary hiatus between parliament and the crown. But it is amazing how easy it was to get over that. Let me recall to you, Sir, that we have on the very first page of Hansard of this year an intimation that a via media exists. The House of Commons was in session; we were sitting, and the Clerk of the House, Arthur Beauchesne, Esquire, B.A., K.C.. proceeded to read to the assembled members a communication-from whom? From the Secretary of the Governor General. We had not cut off communication. His Excellency was able to communicate with us.
He informed us, through Mr. Beauchesne, that the Chief Justice of Canada, in his capacity as Deputy Governor General, would proceed to the Senate chamber on Thursday, the 7t,h of January, at three p.m. That was not the only via media, the only line of communication we had. The awful chaos pictured so eloquently by the hon. member for West Calgary, that vast yawning abyss into which the whole of this parliament was to be hurled for years if we did not recognize the desperate position of the Prime Minister -that he had no power, no office and there was nothing we could do-we find it quite simple to get over that because, you see, Your Honour had been appointed; you had been regularly elected to the office of Speaker by the members assembled here. Parliament met the next day. We were again in communication with His Excellency. His secretary wrote a letter to Mr. Speaker informing him and, through him, this -House, that at three p.m. on Friday, January 8, His Excellency would proceed to the Senate chamber for the purpose of formally opening the session of the Dominion parliament.
So much for the via media. The imaginary difficulties of the via media are as absurd as the situation painted by hon. members on this side of the House who would assure us and the people of Canada that because there was no Prime Minister in the House, the House could not function; the administration could not function; nothing could be done; _ we had better pack up and go back home until the Conservatives came into power. What I would like to know is this: We find there is a via media; that the Speech from the Throne is properly, constitutionally and legally drafted. It is presented to His Excellency. His Excellency calls us together and we walk down to the -Senate chamber, stand humbly before the bar of that noble and august chamber and listen carefully to the reading of the Speech. Then, Mr. Speaker, a messenger walks down with a copy of the Speech to yourself. Your Honour comes back into this House and you read it to the House. Everything is beautiful. Just when did it become illegal for this speech to be read? Just when does the leader of the opposition state it was improper for the Governor General to have sanctioned that Speech? I do not know whether this point has ever struck any hon. member. Just at what point, at what particular instant, did the administration cease to exist, cease to become advisers of the crown, cease to be capable of carrying on as an executive? That has never been told to me. I cannot
Government's Right to Office

ascertain it. and I have read and listened to most of the speeches. We have the Speech read. It is brought into parliament. It is moved that we consider it. No, said the leader of the opposition, there is no government. We cannot consider it. We will not consider it at all; but instead of considering it we shall have a different amendment altogether. We will move that the administration is not competent to carry on:
That those who now assume to be His Excellency's advisers have among them no Prime Minister with a seat in either house of parliament, and under the circumstances are not competent to act as, or to become, the committee of parliament, commonly known as the government, or to address parliament through His Excellency, and their attempted continuance in office is a violation of the principles and practice of British constitutional government.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) endeavouring to prove his point took up a little space. I must say that I have heard few orations in this House that equalled in splendour or volume this sonorous speech of the hon. gentleman. It might be well to note in passing that a column of Hansard is about eight inches in length and that there are eight lines to the inch and two and1 a half inches to the line. So that on this basis the hon. gentleman gave us three hundred and sixty feet of talk in order to prove-what? In. order to prove what Gladstone did in 1845. I can tell the hon. member, if he is bent on tradition, that Gladstone also chopiped wood, and I would recommend that instead of worrying about constitutional traditions the hon. member should adopt that very healthful practice. I notice also that Gladstone practised free trade. How far are the opposition, especially the hon. member for West Calgary, willing to go in putting that theory into practice? We shall find out more about that when the coal policy of this country is before the House for consideration. I want to remind the 'hon. member for Portage la Prairie that Mr. Gladstone was a strong advocate of peace, and I will concede this much, that lately the right hon. gentleman has shown an inclination to adopt Gladstone's traditional policy in this direction. But we must be oareful not to say "Ready, aye, ready," because that would foe jmis-quoting the right hon. gentleman. I have been in this House four years and have listened to the leader of the opposition again and again declare that he had been misquoted, and I have come to the conclusion that there is no more misquoted person in the Dominion of Canada than he is. I do not think it is altogether his fault; it may be due to the stupidity of his reporters. I do not think 
that even the Angel Gabriel will be able to report him properly when he goes up above. I say, I do not think it is due to any fault of the right hon. gentleman; as a rule he is exceedingly clear in his analysis of any situation or of any policy that comes before us. I believe that it is due rather to the darkness of Conservative policy, for it is impossible for any human being, with all the weaknesses of a human being, to make the Conservative policy blear. I read somewhere in a description of a certain lake that it was so dark and so deep that even the eye of God could not see into it. I wonder if the Conservative policy is as dark as that. Can anyone'tell me when the administration actually ceased to function? Did it cease on Thursday before the Speech was read? If it did, then His Excellency had no right to read the Speech because he had no advice. If it did not cease on the Thursday before the Speech was read did it cease while His Excellency was reading the Speeoh? Do you not see what an absurd position we get into? I cannot for the life of me see the logic of it; it puzzles me. It is as deep indeed as the black lake to which I have referred.
The point is made that when parliament met there was no government. That can have no relation to majorities, because on the principle laid down by hon. gentlemen to my right, if the Liberal party had returned with 200 members and still had no Prime Minister they would have had to resign at once: by reason of that fact they would have no government, no via media. They would have to walk out. We see again the absurdity of the thing. It seems to me that it would be well for us to reduce our arguments once in a while to ordinary farmer's horse sense. If we did so we might get a little further ahead than we do by listening to learned dissertations from constitutional lawyers. Let us examine, for instance, the functions of the executive. They are two-fold: first, to advise the crown, and secondly, to execute laws. Both these functions are extra-parliamentary; they are exercised outside parliament altogether. But what are the functions of the executive within parliament? None whatever. The executive in parliament resolves itself into individual members who may consider such legislation as is before the House; but so far as the committee of parliament is concerned it is a mere phrase and that is all. Let me ask hon. members to your left, Mr. Speaker, this question: Does the committee of parliament cease to function because one of its members happens to be absent for a while? Certainly not; any committee of this

Government's Right to Office
parliament appointed by the all-powerful representatives of the people can function so long as it has a quorum. The government therefore were not necessarily under the obligation of resigning simply because they, like hon. gentlemen to your left, Mr. Speaker, did not have a majority over all. That seems clear to me. In the second place,
I do not think that the absence temporarily of the Prime Minister is an essential feature. If any hon. gentleman can show that the Prime Minister deliberately intends to flout his responsibility to parliament; if he can show that the Prime Minister is conspiring against parliament to take advantage of the situation-if any hon. member can produce the proof of this, I will vote for the amendment. But if he cannot produce that evidence, then I say he is not justified in assuming that the Prime Minister intends to remain indefinitely out of parliament, especially when every voice we have heard agrees, as indeed hon. gentlemen to my right know for a positive fact, that the Prime Minister intends to seek a seat at the earliest opportunity and take his place in the House. But let us suppose that this flagrant situation exists as hon. gentlemen suggest, and that after a month or so the Prime Minister is still out of parliament: what then? Why, parliament is still all-powerful and it can instantly rectify any wrong that may exist. There, again, we need to use some common sense. I do not feel justified in supporting the amendment. Apart from what I have said, I cannot regard a vote for the motion itself, as a vote of confidence. I cannot regard this as a vote of confidence. We have the word of the ministry itself that if this amendment is defeated it will not be taken as a vote of confidence, either in the past, the present or the future, and I am willing to accept the ministerial statement to that effect. I personally would not care at this time to vote confidence in the government until I had an opportunity of discussing their policies. But what is the position of my hon. friends to my right? They ask us, inferentially at least, to vote confidence in them without any policy at all, indeed, with a frank statement saying that they will have no dealings with us whatever-no bids, no truck or trade.
No bribery.

Exactly. Nothing whatever. Under these conditions I am not going to be trapped into casting my vote on some trick amendment. I would regret indeed if the government itself should have attempted to trap us; I would regret it just as much
if the opposition attempted to trap us. I intend to reserve my vote for legislation. If I have no confidence in the power of the administration to carry out the legislation, with my assistance, I will have no hesitation in voting them out; and I can assure my hon. friends to my right that when that day comes I will give them just as much consideration, just as fair treatment, as I am willing to give to either party in this House, to assist that party to function and carry on the administration. If the amendment-and this, Mr. Speaker, is the concluding argument which has convinced me of the reasonableness of my position-carried, what would it do? It would aim a loaded gun at the head, the body and the tail of every economic group organization, every individual independent, every little group now endeavouring to take organized citizenship action, every lititle body of individuals coming together and trying to build up their citizenship intelligence to that point where they can once and for all time eliminate the cursed evils of the political party system. It would aim that gun at their heads and at any moment it could be set off.
What does the amendment say? It says in effect that after every election the Governor General should designate as the administration that group which has secured most of the seaits in the House, in other words the major group. That is a vicious principle, and one which for all time- consigns organized democracy to oblivion. I want you to imagine the situation, if Your Honour will. We have a House of 245 members; 45 of them are elected as a major group. The other 200 are divided up into several groups, intelligently organized, trying to take separate political action, separated from campaign funds and the influences of special privilege, trying to undertake the development of true democracy. This amendment says these men shall not get together, but that the little group of 45 is to carry on the administration. Note this:	They Can carry on until parliament meets, which may be months. They may do irreparable harm to the Dominion in that time. It is true that once parliament meets they cannot exist longer, but in the meantime they have held office; they have held the machinery to do many things, to fill many posts, let many contracts and do a great deal of evil. So. Mr. Speaker, having at heart the interests of the organization to which I belong and to which I owe responsibility, the organized farmers of the province of Alberta, I cannot be false to my trust and deliberately assist the opposition in aiming that gun at the head and body of that association, threatening it with utter extinction so far as

political action is concerned. This amendment is infinitely more evil, more far-reaching in its effects, more damning to the democracy of this country than were certain amendments to the Elections Act.

The question is on the
amendment. Before the vote is taken I wish to remind hon. members, that this is a difficult vote to poll on account of the number of new members who are going to take part in it.
